title: Supreme Court Allows White House Ballroom Construction to Proceed
summary: Former White House lawyer Ty Cobb on Monday criticized President Trump's White House ballroom project, stating the historic building is turning into some combination of a whorehouse and Las Vegas. His comments followed the Supreme Court's 5-4 decision on August 31, 2026, allowing construction of the estimated US$400 million White House ballroom to continue. The Court granted an emergency request from the Trump administration, staying lower court rulings that had partially blocked the project. The majority ruled on procedural grounds, finding that the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which brought the legal challenge, likely lacked legal standing to sue because it was not directly harmed by the project. The Court did not address the underlying legality of the construction. Chief Justice John Roberts dissented, joining Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson. Roberts argued the construction was likely unlawful because Congress had not passed any law granting express authority for building on federal park grounds in the District of Columbia. He wrote that "Today's decision is no victory for the separation of powers." President Trump celebrated the ruling on Truth Social, stating he was pleased and that the "Ballroom/Military Complex" would be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C. He said the project would be completed by summer 2028. The 90,000-square-foot ballroom complex involves demolishing the East Wing and includes a military complex underneath with drone-proof structures and drone ports. White House spokesman David Ingle stated the project is inextricably tied to the security of the president, the White House grounds, and the certain security infrastructure assets. Ingle cited a shooting at the White House Correspondents' Dinner in April and a thwarted attack on the UFC Freedom 250 event in June as evidence of the project's necessity.

title: Former UK Prime Minister Starmer Resigns as MP, Focuses on Global Affairs
summary: Sir Keir Starmer announced his departure from the House of Commons on Tuesday, stepping down as the Member of Parliament for Holborn and St Pancras. He told local media he decided over the summer to pivot toward global issues, stating he would now focus on other things, and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world. Starmer also intends to continue his work on combating violence against women and girls, an issue he started before becoming an MP. His resignation triggers an imminent by-election in the central London constituency, a Labour stronghold where he secured a majority of over 11,000 votes in the 2024 general election. Conservative chairman Kevin Hollinrake accused Starmer of making another U-turn having pledged to stay on, prompting a costly by-election for taxpayers. Starmer had previously stated he would remain an MP until the next UK general election, due in 2029. He represented Holborn and St Pancras for 11 years, having taken over from Frank Dobson. Starmer resigned as Prime Minister in June or July, two years after leading the Labour Party to a landslide victory in 2024. Andy Burnham assumed the role of Prime Minister over the summer, replacing Starmer. Prime Minister Burnham paid tribute to Starmer in the House of Commons, telling MPs Starmer gave the UK a lifetime of public service. Starmer's announcement comes hours before Prime Minister Burnham is due to deliver his first statement in the Commons. Foreign affairs were often seen as a strength during Starmer's premiership; he worked with French President Emmanuel Macron to establish the Coalition of the Willing in support of Ukraine, reset ties with China, recognized a Palestinian state, and had mixed success in efforts to build relations with US President Donald Trump.

title: Former Gang Leader Duane Davis Found Guilty of Tupac Shakur Murder
summary: Sekyiwa 'Set' Shakur, the rapper’s sister, cried quietly as the verdict was read in court. Sentencing is scheduled for October 13, and Davis stated his intention to appeal the conviction. A Las Vegas jury deliberated for less than three hours after an 11-day trial in Clark County District Court. Prosecutors argued Davis planned the drive-by shooting after Shakur's entourage attacked his nephew, Orlando 'Baby Lane' Anderson, at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas following a Mike Tyson fight. Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, allegedly supplied the weapon and set the shooting in motion. Nevada law allows conviction for someone who helps commit a murder, even if they did not pull the trigger. Prosecutors said Davis was the shot caller inside the white Cadillac from which Shakur was shot. Shakur, 25, was shot four times on September 7, 1996, and died six days later. Death Row Records co-founder Marion 'Suge' Knight, who was driving the BMW, was wounded. The investigation into Shakur's death was revived after Davis published his memoir, "Compton Street Legend," in 2019, describing his role. Prosecutors also cited a 2008 agreement Davis reached with federal investigators, where he discussed the Shakur shooting, believing it offered immunity. Davis is the only person charged in Shakur's death and the only person still alive among the four men prosecutors say were in the Cadillac. Davis's defense attorney, Michael Sanft, argued the prosecution lacked forensics, eyewitnesses, or physical evidence, relying only on Davis's statements.

title: Bank of America VP Killed in Times Square Stabbing; Suspect Shot Dead
summary: Erin Piacenti, a Bank of America vice-president, was killed in a stabbing at Times Square on Monday. Piacenti, 32, died at the hospital from her injuries. Bank of America stated it was shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of their colleague. The suspect, Pamela Cisneros Lopez, 49, was shot dead by police after the attack. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said a woman carrying multiple knives stabbed two people in Times Square before police used a taser and fired their weapons. NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch called it an unprovoked double stabbing that occurred within approximately 20 seconds. The incident began near West 41st Street and Seventh Avenue at approximately 4:24 PM local time. A witness observed Cisneros Lopez remove two knives from a red Target bag before approaching the first victim, a 68-year-old man who had just exited the subway with his wife. Cisneros Lopez stabbed the 68-year-old man in the right side of his abdomen. He was taken to Bellevue Hospital and is in stable condition. The suspect then continued up Seventh Avenue towards 42nd Street, where she stabbed Piacenti in the abdomen. Officers confronted Cisneros Lopez between 42nd and 43rd streets while she was still armed with both knives. Officers spoke to her for four minutes, telling her to drop the knives, but she refused. Cisneros Lopez told officers, "I'm not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you." Responding officers fired stun guns at her, which did not appear effective. Cisneros Lopez then advanced toward officers, prompting two officers to open fire. She fell to the ground, was handcuffed, and given first aid before being pronounced dead at the hospital. NYPD Commissioner Tisch stated the attacks appeared random and unprovoked, and investigators do not believe the attack was terrorism-related. Cisneros Lopez had a documented mental health history with the department, including two incidents in 2018 and 2019, but no prior arrests. Police have not provided any information about her motive.

title: MapQuest Reaches Top App Store Spot Defying Trump's Lake Ontario Order
summary: MapQuest is now the top free app in the Apple App Store after declining to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America." Interior Secretary Doug Burgum stated President Trump has asked Apple directly to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" on its maps. Burgum expressed confidence that the "Lake America" name could be seen on Apple's platform soon. Apple did not immediately comment on Monday. The order directs the Department of the Interior and the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to formalize the change within 30 days. MapQuest announced its decision on social media on August 27, posting "We're not changing it." The company later posted, "We are aware that Lake Ontario is being correctly labeled on our map." MapQuest also launched a tool allowing people to create their own name for the lake. MapQuest saw more than 100,000 downloads on Sunday alone, its best day in a decade. Daily downloads in the U.S. were up more than 10 times week-on-week in the week beginning August 24. Usage of the app is running roughly 50 times its normal rate. Doug Berger, general manager of MapQuest, stated hundreds of thousands of people signaled they got it right by downloading the app. MapQuest is also currently the No.1 overall free app in the Canadian Apple App Store on the navigation chart. Google Maps updated its maps over the weekend to reflect Mr. Trump's new name for Lake Ontario for U.S. users. A search for "Lake Ontario" on Google now directs people to "Lake America." Google stated its updates follow their long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country. Canadians and some U.S. officials, including the Rochester city council and the Seneca Nation leader, oppose the renaming of Lake Ontario.

title: Spanish Prime Minister Blames Russia, Israel for Ceuta Disinformation
summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez accused networks linked to Russia and Israel of spreading disinformation regarding the migration crisis in Ceuta. Sánchez stated on Monday that these countries were exploiting the issue in retaliation for Madrid's positions on the war in Ukraine and Israel's actions in the Palestinian Territories. He cited research by the European External Action Service (EEAS) but provided no further details; the EEAS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia and Israel have denied their involvement. The migration influx saw over 72,000 migrants cross from Morocco into the autonomous Spanish territory of Ceuta on July 30 and 31. At least 70 people died during these attempted mass-crossings, according to Spain's national EFE news agency. Around 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta at the end of August, including 1,200 minors, Sánchez said. Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas reported 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, since the mass influx, noting this is almost one case daily. Rojas told El País newspaper that migrant girls are particularly vulnerable. Suspected attackers include four Moroccans, three Spaniards, and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports. Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo announced a multi-million euro aid package to provide essential services and care for unaccompanied children. Sánchez has ruled out Moroccan involvement in the migrant surge, stating no intelligence service suggests it. Morocco has renewed demands for Spain to return Ceuta and Melilla. Italy responded to the influx by introducing targeted air and sea border checks for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain, prompting Spain to retaliate with matching temporary border controls.

title: Trump Threatens FCC Action Against NBC Reporter Kristen Welker
summary: President Donald Trump threatened to report NBC's "Meet the Press" host Kristen Welker to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for rebuke or punishment. Trump made the threat in a Sunday morning Truth Social post, reacting to Welker's comment that his primary endorsements yielded mixed results. Trump insisted his endorsement record was "100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House, recently and over the longterm." Trump wrote, "How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves?" He also posted, "I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously." Democratic FCC commissioner Anna Gomez described Trump's threat as dangerous. Former FCC chair Tom Wheeler expressed hope that the agency would stand up for free speech. Wheeler noted that current FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has previously acted as Trump's attack dog, citing instances like reviving a complaint against CBS in January 2025, urging action after Jimmy Kimmel's remarks in September, threatening broadcasters over Iran war coverage in March 2026, and ordering Disney's ABC stations to submit licenses for review in April. Trump also posted on Truth Social about "THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA," calling for "FCC TO THE RESCUE!" Bill Maher publicly apologized on his show for overstating Trump's endorsement losses after receiving a text message from Trump. Maher stated only nine of 260 Trump-endorsed candidates lost, yielding a 97 percent success rate. Trump also attacked New York Times journalist Maggie Haberman, calling her an unattractive person both inside and out and "Maggot Haberman."

summary: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial informed Judge William Sullivan on Tuesday morning that they cannot reach an unanimous verdict. This marks the fourth day of deliberations in the case. Judge Sullivan instructed the jury to continue their deliberations. The jury had met for less than an hour on Tuesday before sending a note to the judge just after 10 a.m. The jury consists of nine women and three men and has deliberated for about 18 hours since receiving the case last Thursday in Plymouth Superior Court. On Friday, the panel requested to see Clancy's prescription pill bottles and the knife she used in her suicide attempt, which were exhibits in the case. Lindsay Clancy, 36, has admitted killing her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan, in their Duxbury home on January 24, 2023. She then slashed her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window in a suicide attempt, leaving her paralyzed from the waist down. Clancy has pleaded not guilty to three counts of first-degree murder, asserting an insanity defense. The central question for the jury is whether Clancy should be held criminally responsible for her actions. Her defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, argues she was not criminally responsible due to being overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors contend Clancy planned the killings and knew right from wrong when she strangled the children. The prosecution noted Clancy had mapped the distance and time for her husband's errands, and she killed her children after he left, citing this as evidence of premeditation. One psychiatrist testified that Clancy's claim of experiencing postpartum psychosis only during the 18-minute window of the killings was inconsistent with the condition. If the jury remains deadlocked, Judge Sullivan will meet with attorneys and then read the "Tuey-Rodriguez" instructions, a last resort in Massachusetts to encourage a verdict.

title: Hague Court Rules India Cannot Unilaterally Suspend Indus Waters Treaty
summary: A court of arbitration in The Hague ruled on Monday that India cannot unilaterally suspend the Indus Waters Treaty, rejecting India's arguments for holding the six-decade-old water-sharing agreement in abeyance since April 2025. The five-member court issued an unanimous decision, finding the treaty remains fully in force and that India must observe its obligations under it. This ruling is the first time an international court has ruled on the legal validity of India's decision to place the treaty in abeyance. The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in The Hague also ordered India to limit construction on the Ratle hydroelectric plant in Kashmir, prohibiting work on the dam wall and power intake structure above certain levels. This order remains in place until 90 days after a World Bank-appointed neutral expert delivers a final decision, expected before July 2027. Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar welcomed the PCA's ruling via social media, stating it vindicates Pakistan's consistent position that a binding international treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended or set aside. India announced its decision to suspend the treaty in April 2025, following a deadly attack on tourists in Indian-administered Kashmir, for which it blamed Pakistan. Islamabad denies involvement in the attack, which killed 26 civilians. The Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank in 1960, governs the use of rivers in the Indus basin, granting India unrestricted access to eastern rivers and Pakistan rights to western rivers. The treaty has endured three wars and prolonged diplomatic tensions. India has rejected the jurisdiction of the PCA in this case, stating that the so-called Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India's sovereign decisions. India's Ministry of External Affairs said its pronouncements will have no effect on India's actions. Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, addressing the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit on Tuesday, described water as the lifeblood of the region and said it must never be weaponized for political leverage. He stated that treaties governing shared waters are solemn binding international commitments that must be honoured unconditionally.

title: Trump Says US Position on Falkland Islands Sovereignty Under Review
summary: United States President Donald Trump said on Monday that he may review his country's position on the sovereignty dispute over the Malvinas Islands between Argentina and the United Kingdom. When asked by reporters in the Oval Office if the U.S. was reviewing its position, Trump replied, "I always review every position. That's just one of many." Trump also commented on the UK's defense funding, stating, "The UK's got some problems, but they'll get solved," when asked if he wanted the government of new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to increase its NATO spending commitments. Reports by British outlet The Telegraph last week indicated that US defense officials were drawing up proposals to incentivize NATO allies to meet spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among possible options. Chancellor John Healey, who oversees the UK's economy and finance ministry, is reportedly delaying Britain's previous commitment to spend 3% of its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on defense by 2030. The Falkland Islands, also known as the Malvinas Islands, are in the south-west Atlantic Ocean and remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina. The two countries fought a 74-day war over the territory in 1982, which resulted in the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders, and 649 Argentine soldiers. Previous US administrations have formally recognized the UK's de facto administration of the islands but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty. In April, an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters suggested the US was considering options to punish NATO allies it believed had failed to support its war in Iran, including reviewing its position on Britain's claim to the Falklands. Trump has pressured US allies to increase their defense spending and NATO contributions, accusing them of freeloading on United States military resources. At the 2025 NATO Summit in The Hague, member states committed to increasing total defense and security spending to 5% of GDP annually by 2035.

title: Norway's King Haakon VIII Swears Oath to Constitution in Parliament
summary: King Haakon VIII pledged an oath of allegiance to Norway's constitution in parliament on Tuesday, marking an important symbolic step as he takes over after his late father's 35-year reign. Haakon became Norway's monarch when King Harald V died on Friday morning at age 89. His wife, Queen Mette-Marit, missed the ceremony due to complications from a lung transplant in June, with their daughter, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, 22, standing by his side. The 53-year-old King Haakon VIII recited, "I promise and swear that I will govern the kingdom of Norway in accordance with its constitution and laws; so help me God, the almighty and omniscient," before cabinet ministers and MPs in the main chamber of the 169-seat parliament. He was driven from the royal palace to the Storting, or parliament, in an open car. Speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the official announcement of Harald's death and Haakon's succession. Dr. Are Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo University Hospital, stated that complications after a lung transplant are not uncommon and Queen Mette-Marit had experienced them on several occasions, including Tuesday, requiring observation. King Harald V died at 89 after a period of ailing health, having faced mounting health problems in his final years. His funeral is scheduled for September 9 in Oslo Cathedral, with heads of state from around the world invited. Tens of thousands of Norwegians have flocked to the royal palace to lay flowers, drawings, candles, and flags in tribute. Norway abolished coronations in 1908, but monarchs can opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral. Haakon has adopted the motto "All for Norway," which dates back to his great-grandfather. Marius Borg Høiby, Queen Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship, who is serving a four-year prison sentence under house arrest after being found guilty on two counts of rape and 30 additional charges, was granted temporary release to attend King Harald V's funeral service on September 9. He was also approved to participate in Monday evening's procession when the King's remains were transferred to the palace chapel.

title: Global Bond Yields Surge to Multi-Year Highs Amid Inflation Fears
summary: Global government bond yields are at or near multi-decade peaks on Tuesday due to heightened worries about inflation and rising interest rates. Japan's 10-year bond yield hit 3% for the first time since 1996, marking a 30-year high. The U.S. 10-year Treasury note yield rose to about 4.79% on Tuesday, its highest level since January 2025. The U.S. 30-year Treasury bond yield was above 5.2% on Tuesday, having risen to its highest since 2007 earlier in August. Germany's 10-year Bund climbed above 3.36% on Tuesday, a 15-year high. The French 10-year OAT yield rose to its highest level since November 2008, and the Dutch 10-year government bond yield increased to 3.43%, its highest since May 2011. The immediate cause for the surge in yields includes renewed tensions in the Middle East, specifically U.S. forces launching strikes against Iran and a tanker being struck off the coast of Oman. These tensions pushed oil prices higher, with Brent crude advancing more than 2% to above $92 per barrel on Tuesday. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh indicated discomfort with the current rate of inflation, which investors interpreted as a signal for likely interest rate increases. Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, UBS chief investment officer, cited no clear path to reopening the Strait after six months of war, elevated inflation worries, Fed policy uncertainty, fiscal concerns, and rising AI-related debt issuance as contributing factors. The U.S. debt pile recently crossed $40 trillion. Eurozone inflation reached 3.3% in August, up from 2.9% in July, with energy prices 14.3% higher year-on-year. Higher borrowing costs are expected for consumers, impacting mortgages, auto loans, and credit card debt.

title: EU Places ChatGPT, Reddit, Roblox Under Stricter Digital Rules
summary: The European Commission on Monday designated ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox under the strictest tier of its online regulations, giving the US-based services four months to comply with new rules. ChatGPT was classified as a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE), while Reddit and Roblox were designated as Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) under the Digital Services Act (DSA). All three reported at least 45 million average monthly users in the EU, exceeding the threshold for heightened oversight. The companies now have until the end of December to comply with additional requirements, including assessing and mitigating systemic risks related to illegal content, minors, users' physical and mental well-being, fundamental rights, elections, and public security. Violations of the DSA can result in fines of up to 6% of a company's annual global turnover. OpenAI and Reddit stated they are preparing to comply with the new requirements, while Roblox pledged to continue working constructively with Brussels. The DSA and its competition-focused sister law, the Digital Markets Act (DMA), have become a source of friction with Washington. US President Donald Trump has ordered officials to scrutinize EU digital rules that could force American companies to moderate content in ways that undermine freedom of speech and political engagement. Vice President J.D. Vance has also accused Europe of retreating from free speech, stating that digital censorship is being presented as a defense of democracy. Separately, the Pentagon announced on Monday that it brought on Starshield AI's Grok for Government and OpenAI's ChatGPT for unclassified military use, expanding the number of AI assistants on the department's platform. The Pentagon stated that Grok for Government will provide the warfighter with immediate information.

title: Iceland Voters Reject Restarting European Union Membership Accession Talks
summary: Iceland's voters rejected reopening European Union membership talks in a referendum on Saturday, with a narrow split of 52.8% to 47.2% against resuming accession negotiations. This result is seen as an uncomfortable reality check for Brussels, which had hoped a hazardous world would make the EU more attractive. Nicola Procaccini, co-chair of the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists group, stated that the Icelandic people's choice not to take even the first step should give Brussels pause. The vote is not a death blow to the 450 million-strong bloc, as Iceland has fewer than 400,000 people and a smaller GDP than Estonia. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made no public statement, with an anonymous spokesperson saying Brussels had taken note of the results. European Council President António Costa, through his spokesperson, said the EU fully respects the democratic choice of the Icelandic people. Dagur Eggertsson, an MP and former Mayor of Reykjavík, noted a very harsh campaign with a lot of money, echoing the "Brexit playbook." Talks with the EU to join the bloc had begun after the 2008 financial crisis but had been suspended. The referendum pitted concerns about geopolitical stability against keeping national control of Iceland's prized fisheries. Iceland's government had asked Brussels not to interfere in what Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir stressed was a domestic matter. The government confirmed it will not restart EU accession negotiations during its term. EU officials had hoped a "Yes" vote would be an endorsement of Europe's attractiveness in the world. John Fund of The Spectator noted that elites in Reykjavik were the only part of the country to vote "Yes," and that a majority of voters did not see why Iceland should be shackled to a European superstate that could dilute its sovereignty and control over fishing waters.

title: Fed Chair Warsh Signals Hawkish Stance, Markets React to Hike Bets
summary: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh gave his first major speech as chairman on August 28 at this year's Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium, signaling an unexpectedly hawkish stance that boosted market expectations for a rate hike next month. Global markets traded mostly lower at the start of the week, with stocks sinking and oil jumping on Warsh's comments and US-Iran strikes. Traders of fed funds futures now see a 60.4% chance of a quarter-point hike in September. Gold fell and Asian stocks declined on Monday following the speech. JPMorgan traders dropped their bullish view on stocks after Warsh's remarks. Barclays forecasts two Fed rate hikes after the Jackson Hole speech. Warsh told G20 finance leaders on Monday that the world is seeing a global investment surge that is helping to power growth, reversing past savings gluts. The highlight is the Federal Reserve chair's annual address, usually given on Friday morning. Paul Volcker was the first Fed chair to attend in 1982, and Alan Greenspan was a regular opening speaker for over 14 years. Jerome Powell, Warsh's immediate predecessor, frequently used his annual address to foreshadow Fed policy. Warsh explained that forward guidance, the practice of broadcasting monetary policy moves in advance, became a regular practice during the global financial crisis to maintain market calm. However, the current Fed chair believes it has overstayed its welcome, as markets have become too reliant on this information, potentially locking the central bank into foreshadowed policies regardless of changing circumstances. President Donald Trump declined to criticize Warsh for suggesting a potential rate increase, stating he trusts his appointee will do what he has to do, but also said he thinks interest rates are too high.

title: Israel, Greece Sign $3.5 Billion Defense Deal for Air Shield
summary: Israel and Greece finalized a $3.5 billion defense deal on Monday, providing Greece with a multilayered antimissile system called "Achilles Shield." The agreement, signed at Tel Aviv's Ministry of Defense, is one of the largest defense export deals in Israel's history. Maj. Gen. Amir Baram, director-general of Israel's Defense Ministry, and Maj. Gen. Ioannis Bouras of Greece signed the agreement. The deal, valued at approximately 3 billion euros ($3.5 billion), will see Israel build a comprehensive, multi-layered air defense array in Greece, drawing entirely on Israeli-made systems. These systems include David's Sling and SPYDER, manufactured by Rafael, and BARAK MX, manufactured by Israel Aerospace Industries. An additional 26 million euro agreement was signed for the sale of Rafael's Drone Dome air defense systems to Greece. The deal also provides for expanded defense industrial cooperation, including the transfer of knowledge and technology to local industry. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz stated that the two countries share common strategic interests and face shared regional challenges. He added that Israel and Greece will continue to deepen their defense and strategic cooperation to preserve stability and safeguard shared interests. This agreement is a direct continuation of the Eastern Mediterranean alliance forged a decade ago with Greece and southern Cyprus. title: Shein Shares Slide on Hong Kong Market Debut Amid Scrutiny
summary: Shares in the fast-fashion brand Shein slumped by as much as 10% on Tuesday as the China-founded company made its trading debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange. The company priced its shares at HK$48.56 each, valuing the business at just over $26 billion. Minutes after the flotation, which raised HK$13.6 billion ($1.7 billion), the stock fell to as low as HK$43.72 before recovering most of its early losses. Shein's shares closed at HK$48.50, down just 0.12% from its opening price. The company was once estimated to be worth nearly $100 billion in 2022, but its value has dropped by one-fourth to an IPO valuation of $26.5 billion. Shein reported a $99 million loss in its first quarter. Chief financial officer Leigh Gui stated that the company's model of selling large numbers of small orders with rapid payment options now reaches about 160 markets worldwide. Shein has more than 273 million active customers who placed over a billion orders in the year to the end of March 2026. Shein's attempts to list in the UK and US were reportedly scuppered by supply chain concerns and criticism of its environmental impact and alleged forced labor. The plunge in its value has also been driven by regulatory changes worldwide that threaten its business model of shipping goods in small packages out of China to take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods. France began imposing penalties on the extreme end of fast fashion on Tuesday to curb sales of cheap clothing from e-commerce sites like Shein and Temu. These penalties, part of a fast-fashion law passed in June, aim to address environmental concerns from overproduction and range from 0.25 euros to 12 euros per item, capped at 50% of the product's pre-tax sales price. China's commerce ministry described the French law as discriminatory and a trade barrier. Separately, tram services between Wan Chai and Admiralty in Hong Kong were suspended Tuesday night due to a power failure, the second such incident in two days.

title: Trump Defends Hosting Russian Finance Minister at G20 Amid European Disapproval
summary: United States President Donald Trump defended having Russia at the G20 finance meeting on Monday, amid backlash from European officials who disapproved of the move. Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov made a surprise appearance at the meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, marking his first in-person G20 attendance since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. European leaders were irked by the move, with some reportedly refusing to participate in a group photograph if Siluanov was included. German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil called the decision to treat Siluanov as a regular participant a troubling signal. Trump told reporters, "We're going to see what happens, but we like getting along with everybody. One of the reasons that I'm so successful, I get along with everybody." US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with Siluanov on the sidelines of the event. Russia's Finance Ministry stated the pair discussed Russia-U.S. Cooperation on financial matters and interaction within the G20 framework. A Treasury spokesperson told Axios that Bessent and Siluanov spoke about Trump's Ukraine peace plan and economic growth, adding that Bessent ruled out economic relief for Moscow as long as the war in Ukraine continues. title: Eurozone Inflation Rises to 3.3 Percent in August, Rate Hike Expected
summary: Eurozone inflation rose to 3.3 percent in August, according to a preliminary estimate published by Eurostat on Tuesday. This figure is above July's 2.9 percent rate and marks the highest level in three years, leaving inflation farther from the European Central Bank's (ECB) 2 percent target. Energy costs accounted for most of the acceleration, with annual energy inflation climbing from 10.3 percent in July to 14.3 percent in August. The increase in energy prices reflects disruption to oil and gas markets caused by the conflict in the Middle East, including the Iran war and the near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Traders have locked in expectations for the ECB to hike interest rates at its September 10 meeting, with market pricing on Tuesday morning putting a 98.9 percent probability on a 25 basis point increase to 2.5 percent. The ECB raised its key rate to 2.25 percent in June, its first hike since 2023, in response to global inflationary pressures. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol, and tobacco, dipped to 2.4 percent in August from 2.5 percent in July. Services inflation eased from 3.3 percent to 3 percent, while food, alcohol, and tobacco inflation remained at 1.2 percent. Non-energy industrial goods inflation edged up from 0.9 percent to 1.2 percent. The measure excluding energy was 2.2 percent, considerably below the headline figure. Christine Lagarde, the ECB's chief, warned in July that the energy shock from the conflict could intensify further. Joe Nellis, head of economic research at MHA, stated the ECB will be wary that short-term inflation pressures become structural, feeding into wages and services inflation. Kamil Kovar at Moody's Analytics added that the ECB will hike again next week. German inflation rose to 2.9 percent in August, coming in below expectations.

title: NASA Launches Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on SpaceX Falcon Heavy
summary: NASA launched its Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on Sunday, August 30, aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. Liftoff occurred at 07:26:49 a.m. EDT (11:26:49 GMT) from Launch Complex-39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The telescope is now on its way to an orbital sweet spot nearly 1 million miles from Earth, or 1.5 million kilometers from Earth. It aims to usher in a new wave of discovery into phenomena like dark matter and dark energy. The observatory stands more than 12 meters tall. The launch opportunity was an instantaneous launch window, requiring precise timing down to the second for proper orbital delivery. The telescope is described as the most powerful cosmic surveyor ever sent into space. United States President Donald Trump hailed a "Golden Age of America" as NASA launched the new space telescope. Photos from the telescope are not expected until 2027.

title: Trump Warns Communities Opposing Data Centers Will Be "Backwards and Poor"
summary: United States President Donald Trump has publicly supported the expansion of data centers, warning that communities rejecting them will end up backwards and poor. In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump stated, "If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign." He added that "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement." Trump's intervention comes amid growing opposition across the country to resource-intensive server farms. A longtime Texas Republican voter, Tom Weeks, 66, reacted angrily to Trump's comments, calling them bulls--t rhetoric and insulting as hell on CNN. Weeks, who lives in Granbury, Texas, has pledged to vote for Democrats in the midterms over data center concerns. A UT/TPPP poll found that 57 percent of Texas voters either strongly or somewhat oppose construction of the centers in their community. The US is currently building hundreds of data centers, with one estimate pointing to more than 3,000 operating facilities over the next decade. Major developers include Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta, Oracle, OpenAI, QTS, Digital Realty, Equinix, and CyrusOne. Training and operating frontier AI models requires enormous computing capacity, making data centers power-intensive industrial plants. According to a December 2024 report from Virginia's Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (JLARC), a typical 250,000-square-foot data center project employs roughly 50 full-time workers, with about half being contractors. Brookings reported that a county adds roughly 2,000 to 4,000 additional private-sector jobs about six years after its first large data center opens. Greg Wright, an economist at University of California Merced and a nonresident senior fellow at Brookings institution, stated that many of those jobs are filled by outside contractors rather than local workers. States have offered data centers large targeted tax breaks even as local job gains remain modest, according to an August academic paper co-authored by Wright.

title: Niger Junta Thwarts Mutiny With Help From Russia's Africa Corps, Algeria
summary: Niger's military government thwarted a mutiny by disgruntled soldiers over the weekend, with assistance from Russia's Africa Corps mercenaries and Algeria. The unrest began overnight from Friday, August 28, to Saturday, August 29, with junior officers targeting the presidency, national television, and Base Aérienne 101 near Niamey’s international airport. Mody said the prompt reaction of the defense and security forces made it possible to contain this heated moment. Reporters in Niamey indicated that mutineers remained in control of Air Base 101 until late Saturday afternoon. General Abdourahamane Tiani, the junta boss, maintained power by deploying his loyal presidential guard and receiving help from the Africa Corps, formerly known as the Wagner Group. Viktor Voropaïev, Russian ambassador to Niger, stated that the Nigerien government requested Russia's assistance in quelling the mutiny. title: DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Exceeds 6,000 Cases, Nears 3,000 Deaths
summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) has surpassed 6,000 confirmed cases and resulted in 2,911 deaths as of August 31, according to government figures published on Monday. This outbreak is now the largest recorded in DR Congo's history, exceeding the country's 2018-2020 epidemic. The case fatality rate stands at 48.2 percent. The World Health Organization (WHO) warned on Friday that the outbreak continues to worsen, with cases and deaths rising due to sustained transmission and geographic expansion. The outbreak, declared in May, is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are currently no approved vaccines or specific treatments. It has spread to 60 health zones across six provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele, and Tshopo. Ituri remains the worst affected, with 28 of its 36 health zones reporting cases, and 4,802 confirmed cases recorded as of August 26. A total of 1,366 patients have recovered, while 619 remain in isolation or hospital. Five Ebola survivors, including a healthcare worker, were discharged from treatment in Béni on Sunday. Children across DR Congo returned to school on Tuesday, prompting concern among parents and teachers in Ituri province. Dieudonne Lotsima, a father of three in Bunia, Ituri's provincial capital, questioned whether schools should reopen without a specific vaccine. The Lagos State Government in Nigeria conducted a strategic assessment of its Infectious Disease Hospital, Mainland Hospital, Yaba, to ensure emergency readiness for any possible Ebola Virus Disease outbreak. Akin Abayomi, Lagos State Commissioner for Health, stated the assessment was necessary as the state Ministry of Health prepares for any eventualities. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) head of delegation, Ariel Kestens, stated that sustained attention and resources for the Ebola response in DRC remain essential.

title: Lionel Richie Hospitalized After St. Louis Concert Performance
summary: Singer Lionel Richie checked himself into a local hospital over the weekend following his performance in St. Louis on Saturday night. He subsequently postponed performances in Chicago and Columbus, Ohio, under advisement by doctors to rest and return to full health. Richie returned to the stage on June 30 for a performance in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. In July, he joked about needing electrolytes between songs during a show at Madison Square Garden. Richie was the lead singer and songwriter of the Commodores in the 1970s before going solo in the early 1980s. He co-wrote "We Are The World" in 1985 with Michael Jackson, which raised millions for famine relief in Ethiopia. He has been a judge on "American Idol" since 2018.

title: Oil Prices Rise, US Stocks Fall Amid Renewed US-Iran Fighting
summary: Oil prices rose on Monday, leading to a drop in US stock futures and putting pressure on bond markets, amid renewed fighting between the United States and Iran. Brent crude prices jumped over 2.5 percent on Monday, reaching $90.34 per barrel, with futures for September delivery gaining 3.3 percent to trade at $90.99 a barrel. Iran retaliated, marking the first open fire between the two countries since July. The US-Israeli assault has caused oil prices to spike amid Iran's closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz shipping lane. The Strait of Hormuz is a key energy trade route, with oil flowing from it amounting to 20 percent of the world’s supply. title: UN Panel Urges States to Confront Slavery's Legacy With Reparations
summary: A UN committee has called on countries to adopt comprehensive reparations for people of African descent, asserting that the legacy of the transatlantic slave trade continues to fuel systemic racism and racial inequality. The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination stated in guidance published Monday that governments have legal obligations to address the enduring consequences of the slave trade and racialized slavery, and that the passage of time cannot be used to avoid this responsibility. This represents a shift from arguments over historical responsibility that have often been used to resist reparations claims. The 18-member committee urged governments to combine financial and non-financial remedies, including compensation, restitution, rehabilitation, official recognition, and guarantees against future abuses. They called for national action plans developed in consultation with affected communities and for the repeal or amendment of discriminatory laws. The committee highlighted that the effects of slavery remain visible in systemic discrimination and structural inequalities in education, healthcare, economic opportunity, and environmental security, as well as in racialized violence and institutional barriers. Countries involved directly or indirectly in the transatlantic slave trade have a present-day legal obligation to provide broad reparations, the committee stated.

summary: Andrew Bailey, chair of the Financial Stability Board (FSB), has warned that cyber risk from frontier artificial intelligence poses the most immediate concern to the global financial system. title: US Removes Syria from State Sponsors of Terrorism List
summary: The United States formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism on Monday, rescinding a decades-old designation. The US Department of State also revoked its designation of the al-Nusra Front, later known as Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a global terrorist organization. Al-Sharaa led HTS, which spearheaded the offensive that toppled longtime Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad in 2024. HTS was formerly the branch of Al-Qaeda in Syria before breaking ties in 2016. Syria was first placed on the list in December 1979 during President Jimmy Carter's administration due to the al-Assad regime's support for Palestinian armed groups and its alliance with Tehran. The designation carried restrictions including bans on US foreign assistance and arms exports, controls on dual-use exports, and limits on financial and commercial dealings. The US had initially announced its intent to delist Syria in July, a move seen as a vote of confidence in al-Sharaa. Al-Sharaa met Trump at the White House in November 2025, accelerating the thaw between the two countries. title: Trump Administration Proposes New $103,265 Fee for H-1B Visas
summary: The Trump administration proposed a new $103,265 fee for employers filing cap-subject H-1B petitions, less than three months after a federal judge struck down an earlier $100,000 H-1B payment requirement. The H-1B visa allows US employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations, such as tech and finance. It would not apply to cap-exempt petitions, such as those for foreign workers employed by nonprofit or governmental research organizations or educational institutions. The payment would be in addition to existing fees. DHS projects the annual revenue collected from these petitions to be about $8.8 billion, which would support immigration-related activities across several federal agencies, including US Citizenship and Immigration Services, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, the Justice Department's immigration courts, the State Department, and the Labor Department. Last September, the administration announced a $100,000 fee, which a federal judge in the US District Court for Massachusetts, Leo Sorokin, ruled unlawful in June, calling it a disguised tax. The government appealed, but an appellate court declined to stay Sorokin’s ruling. title: Forensic Psychologist Continues Testimony, Rejects Lindsay Clancy Insanity Defense Claim
summary: Forensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun is scheduled to continue his testimony Tuesday in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy. Heilbrun, who evaluated Clancy for prosecutors, testified Monday that he rejects her claim of killing her three children while following commands from a male voice during a postpartum psychotic episode. He concluded Clancy had experienced intrusive thoughts about killing herself for months and decided to attempt suicide in early 2023, taking her children with her because she was convinced that they would suffer without her. Heilbrun described Clancy's account of the command hallucination as very unusual, noting she never heard the voice before or after strangling 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan. Heilbrun is the second witness for prosecutors, rebutting defense mental health experts who testified last week that Clancy should not be held criminally responsible. The defense asserts an insanity defense, arguing Clancy was in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she strangled her children in January 2023. Prosecutors maintain her actions were calculated and methodical. Jurors are expected to begin deliberations this week, with closing arguments anticipated Wednesday. On Monday, Judge William Sullivan denied a defense request for a mistrial after Heilbrun mentioned Clancy's Catholic faith and her expectation of being together in heaven with God with her children. Judge Sullivan reprimanded the prosecution for the religious reference and instructed jurors to disregard it. This marks the second instance religion has been raised during the trial. Heilbrun also testified that Clancy has bipolar disorder and experienced anxiety, depression, insomnia, and suicidal thoughts in the weeks before the killings. Another forensic psychiatrist, Dr. Avram Mack, previously testified for the prosecution, concluding Clancy had neither bipolar disorder nor psychosis. After the killings, Clancy jumped from a second-floor window and remains paralyzed from the waist down.

title: Stock Futures Fall as Investors Await Fed Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole Speech
summary: Stock futures fell on Monday, weighed by declines in tech shares, following a losing week as markets remain pressured by elevated Treasury yields. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures traded 136 points lower, while S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 futures lost 0.3% and 0.7% respectively. Investors await Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's keynote speech at the annual Jackson Hole symposium this week. The 30-year U.S. Treasury bond yield topped 5.3% last week, reaching levels not seen in nearly 20 years. Treasury yields moved lower Monday, with the 10-year Treasury note yield more than 2 basis points lower at 4.7120%, and the 30-year Treasury note yield dropping more than 2 basis points to 5.2497%. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced measures last week to help stabilize the long-end of the U.S. yield curve, including sharply ramping up purchases of treasury bonds. The rise in treasury yields has sharply increased the cost of servicing the federal debt, which has ballooned to a record $40 trillion. This year, interest payments will absorb 13.5% of all federal spending, up from 5.2% in 2021. President Donald Trump has called interest rates ridiculous and artificially high, blaming the Federal Reserve for not cutting them. Higher treasury yields set the benchmark for rates on mortgage loans and other long-term lending, with fixed rates on thirty-year home loans rising from about six percent to about 6.75 percent since the start of this year. summary: US Republican leader Mike Rogers and his allies have reportedly asked the pro-Israel lobby American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) not to run a campaign on his behalf ahead of the November general election. title: FDA Approves New Blood Test for Alzheimer's Disease Detection
summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new blood test to detect signs of Alzheimer’s disease. Roche announced Sunday that the FDA granted approval to its Elecsys Phospho-Tau blood test for diagnosing Alzheimer’s disease. This marks the fourth such blood test approved in less than two years. The FDA cleared the Elecsys Phospho-Tau (217P) Plasma blood test, developed by Roche and Eli Lilly, on Monday. Roche and Lilly state this is a single-biomarker blood test designed to test for the likelihood of amyloid pathology, a brain symptom linked with Alzheimer’s disease. The test is designed to help identify symptoms related to Alzheimer’s disease in patients over age 55. Doctors previously diagnosed amyloid pathology using PET imaging or cerebrospinal fluid testing, which are described as expensive and invasive procedures. The new test is designed to be minimally invasive and to work easily alongside existing laboratory workflows, not requiring labs to purchase additional equipment, according to Roche and Lilly. However, the test is not designed to be a standalone diagnostic for Alzheimer’s and should be interpreted for patients with other clinical information. Both Labcorp and Quest Diagnostics, large companies offering blood testing services, plan to offer the new test. The FDA previously cleared the first blood test for Alzheimer’s last May. That test, developed by Japanese biotech firm Fujirebio, also tests for amyloid plaques in plasma and can reliably predict amyloid pathology. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates 6.7 million older adults live with diagnosed Alzheimer’s disease in the U.S., making it the most common form of dementia, comprising 60% to 80% of all cases. The CDC projects this figure will double by 2060.

title: Secret White House Bunker Undermines Trump's $600 Million Ballroom Security Case
summary: Former officials state the White House complex already has a secret bunker, undermining President Donald Trump’s security justification for his $600 million White House ballroom. Three ex-officials point to the existence of this nuclear-proof underground base. The bunker, commissioned after the 9/11 attacks and completed during Barack Obama’s tenure, is situated 60 feet below street level. It is accessible by private elevator, stores a month’s supply of food, and has its own air supply system, intended to shield inhabitants from threats including weapons of mass destruction. This facility succeeded the Presidential Emergency Operations Center in the East Wing basement, built for Franklin D Roosevelt in the Second World War. Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Army Secretary Dan Driscoll told the Supreme Court the underground facility is essential to continuity of government and a nondiscretionary prerequisite. Chief Justice John Roberts issued an order Friday allowing construction to continue while the Supreme Court weighs the case. Lower courts had previously halted construction except for national-security-related work. The ballroom project, initially a $200 million event-space renovation, has grown to $600 million, with taxpayers expected to cover over half. summary: Shein will debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange on September 1, targeting a valuation close to $27 billion. summary: Stock futures fell on Monday, weighed by declines in tech shares, following a losing week as markets remain pressured by elevated Treasury yields. title: New Zealand Introduces Legislation to Ban Social Media for Under-16s
summary: New Zealand's government introduced legislation on Monday to ban under-16s from using social media. The proposed law would fine firms like Meta up to 10% of their global revenue if they fail to comply. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon stated, "We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children." Luxon cited that one in three children aged between 13 and 17 spend at least five hours on social media daily. He said social media exposes children to harmful content, addictive technology, and pressures they are not equipped to deal with, affecting family life, mental health, sleep, and education. Luxon specifically named Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, and Facebook, stating they would be required to take reasonable steps to check users are over the age of 16. Verification methods would include existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services and formal ID. Platforms would also need to assess risks and report on danger reduction efforts. Education Minister Erica Stanford said the bill places legal obligations on platforms and proposes no penalties for children, their parents or caregivers. The bill's passage faces uncertainty as National Party's coalition partners, the libertarian ACT party and populist NZ First, oppose it. NZ First stated they could not support the law due to the colossal failure of similar legislation in Australia. ACT believes the law won't work and teenagers would easily circumvent the ban. The main opposition party, Labour, submitted dozens of questions before deciding on support, including how age verification will work and which platforms will be affected. Australia implemented world-first legislation banning children from social media in December, with the UK and France following suit. A June peer-reviewed study by Australian researchers found little evidence that Australia's ban reduced teen social media use. title: Kazakhstan Pro-Government Adilet Party Wins Parliamentary Election with 71 Percent
summary: Kazakhstan’s electoral commission announced Monday that the pro-government Adilet party won more than 71 percent of the vote in Sunday’s parliamentary election. Critics, however, argue the new body will only further cement President Tokayev's power. Kazakhstan’s Supreme Court ruled last month that the new constitution permits Tokayev to run for a new seven-year term. The election occurred amidst soaring inflation, around 10.2%, and rising taxes, raising concerns about potential unrest similar to January 2022, which resulted in 238 deaths. title: US Envoy Walks Back Golan Heights Comments Contradicting Trump Policy
summary: U.S. special envoy to Syria and ambassador to Turkey, Tom Barrack, walked back his comments on Sunday regarding the Golan Heights. Two days prior, on Friday, Barrack had stated that Israel still occupies the Golan Heights in violation of UN resolutions. These remarks contradicted U.S. President Donald Trump's established position on the disputed territory. Barrack clarified his comments, explaining he was referring to the territory’s historical status. In a statement to The Associated Press, Barrack affirmed, "United States policy on the Golan was set by President Trump in 2019 and is unchanged," adding his remarks were not an endorsement of the United Nations’ position. Israel captured the Golan Heights during the 1967 Six-Day War and extended sovereignty over it in 1981. UN Security Council resolution 497, passed shortly after the 1981 annexation, rejected it as null and void. Barrack's initial comments prompted Defense Minister Israel Katz to point out the contradiction with U.S. recognition of Israeli sovereignty. Katz described Barrack's remarks as riddled with inaccuracies and positions that contradict those of U.S. President Trump himself. The comments also drew criticism in Washington, with Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) suggesting Barrack had forgotten Trump’s recognition. On March 25, 2019, President Trump signed Proclamation 9852 recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the strategic plateau. On August 10, 2026, Colombia's Foreign Ministry recognized Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, becoming the second country to officially endorse Jerusalem's claim. Syria has never rescinded its claim to the Golan Heights, and the issue re-entered the spotlight after Ahmed al-Sharaa took power in December 2024. During recent negotiations in Jordan, the Syrian delegation requested to separate talks over the Golan Heights, prioritizing Israel's withdrawal from areas captured after December 2024.

title: DR Congo Battles Ebola Outbreak, Government and M23 Rebels Agree Peace Roadmap
summary: Pope Leo called for international action on Sunday to confront the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo), where thousands have died. DR Congo’s Health Ministry figures show 5,375 confirmed cases and 2,557 deaths, with a 47.6% case fatality rate. The outbreak, the country’s 17th, is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which no licensed vaccine or specific treatment exists. The World Health Organization (WHO) described it as the largest ever recorded in DR Congo, expanding faster than containment efforts. United Nations Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis warned that violence against healthcare workers is hampering the response, with over 260 attacks in six months, killing eight workers. Harneis stated the epidemic, with 2,606 deaths among 5,458 confirmed cases, is growing exponentially. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) also warned the outbreak is out of control and is the fastest moving Ebola epidemic seen. On Friday, Kinshasa received 16,520 Ervebo vaccines, with 50,120 expected by August 24, though these were developed against a different Ebola virus species. Separately, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group agreed on a roadmap for peace talks following discussions in Switzerland from August 17 to 21. The roadmap defines successive stages and a timetable for negotiations under the Doha framework, aiming for a comprehensive peace agreement. Both sides committed to a standardized method for reporting alleged ceasefire violations. A first ceasefire verification mission under the MCVE+ mechanism is scheduled for Monday in Minembwe, South Kivu province. The United States welcomed progress in the Doha peace process, with senior adviser Massad Boulos expressing encouragement. The Doha agreement, signed last year, aimed to establish foundations for peace, including prisoner exchanges and humanitarian access, but fighting has continued. Earlier this month, DR Congo authorities released 15 prisoners to M23.

title: Syrian Court Sentences Former Grand Mufti Ahmad Hassoun to Life in Prison
summary: A Syrian court on Monday handed a life sentence to Ahmad Hassoun, the country's former grand mufti under ex-President Bashar Assad. The Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus found Hassoun guilty of multiple crimes, including inciting sectarian unrest, justifying murder, inciting violence, prolonging killings, and abusing his office. Hassoun served as Syria's top Islamic cleric for 16 years, from 2005 until 2021, and vocally supported the Assad regime's policies. He is the 10th Assad-era official to be sentenced under Syria's new authorities. The court imposed several prison sentences for various charges, including 20 years for inciting killings and 10 years for prolonging killings. Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan stated that Hassoun and the official religious institution he led provided religious cover for military and security operations during al-Assad’s rule. His teachings justified the use of barrel bombs that targeted civilian areas, which constitutes a violation of international humanitarian law. Hassoun was arrested at Damascus airport in March 2025, after emerging from hiding a month earlier, and his trial began on June 25. Bashar Assad has resided in Russia since the fall of his regime in late 2024. A judicial agreement signed by Syria and Russia on June 29, 2022, and ratified by Assad that year, provides a legal avenue for seeking his extradition, though the death sentence itself could give Moscow grounds to refuse.

title: Israel Finds Altalena Ship Intact on Mediterranean Seafloor After 78 Years
summary: Israel announced Monday it had recovered the wreckage of the Altalena, an arms-smuggling boat, found intact on the Mediterranean seafloor 78 years after its sinking. The sinking of the Altalena in 1948 by the Israeli military exposed deep divisions and is described as a painful and seminal event that shook the young State of Israel. The ship had sailed from France carrying weapons for the Irgun, a militant Zionist force. In June 1948, Israeli forces opened fire and sank the boat off Tel Aviv on the orders of David Ben Gurion, Israel's first prime minister. Ben Gurion sought to assert his authority and prevent a paramilitary rival to the newly established Israeli military. Sixteen Irgun members and three Israeli soldiers were killed in the fighting. Irgun chief Menachem Begin instructed his fighters to surrender, famously stating, "There will be no civil war with the enemy at our gates." Begin later became prime minister in 1977. title: Amnesty International Reveals India Used Lethal Weapons on Protesters
summary: An investigation by human rights group Amnesty International confirmed on Monday that Indian government forces used lethal weapons, including pellet-firing shotguns, grenades, batons, and electric shock devices, against demonstrators in Gen Z protests last month in New Delhi. title: Federal Officials Order Major Colorado River Water Cuts for Three States
summary: Federal authorities announced Friday water restrictions for three Western states that rely on the Colorado River, effective over the next two years. Under the Bureau of Reclamation's strategy, California, Nevada, and Arizona will collectively reduce water consumption by 1.25 million acre-feet (approximately 1.54 billion cubic meters) per year. Arizona faces the most substantial reductions among the three states. Upstream states, specifically Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, and New Mexico, will not be subjected to any cutbacks at present. Neighboring Mexico is also set to decrease its water allocation by 250,000 acre-feet (approximately 310 million cubic meters) under a cross-border treaty with the U.S. Andrea Travnicek, the Interior Department’s assistant secretary for water and science, stated that the region has been in a "26-year prolonged drought period" and expects a continued prolonged drought in the future. The existing framework regulating waterway use is set to expire in October, and the seven basin states have not yet reached a consensus on a long-term sharing agreement. Decades of excessive extraction, combined with persistent drought and rising temperatures, have depleted the nation's two largest reservoirs fed by the Colorado River. Lake Mead recently dropped to its lowest point since it was filled nine decades ago, and Lake Powell hit its own record low roughly a week later. Their combined reserves stand at their lowest level in nearly seven decades. The Colorado River Basin experienced the worst snowpack on record last winter, increasing pressure on agriculture, commercial industry, ecological habitats, and hydroelectric producers, as well as tens of millions of consumers, including dozens of Native American tribes and two states in Mexico. Water officials in Arizona thanked California and Nevada for their collaboration on how to divide the required cutbacks. Decades ago, Arizona secured funding for a major Colorado River project by agreeing to be the first to face cuts during a severe drought, a condition the Trump administration now states has been met.

Captain Pat Cummins contributed 3-10 in the second innings, and Nathan Lyon took 3-25. Australia's victory was completed inside two days, making it only the 28th two-day Test in the 2632-match history of Test cricket. This marks the third Test involving Australia in their last seven to finish within two days. Australia's first innings total of 210 was the fourth-lowest in Test history to secure an innings win. All-rounder Cameron Green followed his century in the first Test in Darwin with a gutsy 67" in the second Test, helping Australia to a 146-run lead. Paceman Shoriful Islam claimed 7-48 for Bangladesh, marking the best figures by a Bangladeshi bowler in an away Test. The win comes after Bangladesh had stunned Australia with a nine-wicket victory in the opening Test in Darwin, their first-ever Test win Down Under. Despite the loss in Mackay, Bangladesh climbed three places to No.6 in the latest ICC Test rankings, their highest-ever position. title: Magnitude 5.9 Earthquake Rattles Eastern Japan, Injuring Dozens Near Tokyo
summary: A magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck eastern Japan early Sunday, causing strong shaking and injuring at least 37 people. The quake hit around 2:00 a.m. local time, centered in the southern part of Ibaraki Prefecture at a depth of 68 to 70 kilometers. The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) reported no concern about tsunamis. The tremor registered lower 5 on Japan’s seven-point shindo seismic scale in parts of Ibaraki, Saitama, and Chiba prefectures, as well as in Tokyo’s Adachi Ward. Level 4 shaking was recorded in other areas of Tokyo, Tochigi, Gunma, and Kanagawa prefectures. Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency reported at least 37 injuries across five prefectures: 15 in Tokyo, nine in Saitama, eight in Kanagawa, four in Chiba, and one in Ibaraki. One person sustained serious injuries, including a woman in her 80s who suffered a serious hip injury after falling off her bed in Yokohama, Kanagawa prefecture. Most injuries occurred as people fell or hit furniture after being caught off guard while sleeping. One building was damaged in Saitama Prefecture. The earthquake disrupted some regional train services in Tokyo, with some trains running at reduced speeds. Keisei Line services returned to normal after 9:40 a.m., but some Tobu Railway express services remained halted. Shinkansen bullet trains, however, ran normally. An underground water pipe ruptured in Tokyo’s Koto Ward, with water pouring onto the road, but it was later repaired. The quake also caused blackouts to about 460 homes in Tokyo, with power restored later Sunday morning. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi stated that the government set up a task force to assess the extent of possible damage and urged residents to remain vigilant for the possibility of another earthquake of a similar magnitude for about a week.

title: Kazakhstan Holds First Kurultai Election Amidst Constitutional Reforms
summary: Kazakhstan held its first elections to the unicameral Kurultai on Sunday, August 23, marking a new stage in the country's transition to a single-chamber legislature. Over 12 million of Kazakhstan’s 20 million people were eligible to vote, with 10,363 polling stations opened across the country and 79 stations in 61 foreign countries. Voter turnout reached 37.05 percent as of noon on August 23, with 4,670,816 voters having received ballots. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev cast his ballot at polling station No. 520, describing it as a historic day" and an important historical event" for the country. The election follows constitutional overhauls earlier this year that abolished Kazakhstan’s upper house, the Senate, in favor of the new one-body parliament, the Kurultai. Officials claim this change will give parliament more weight in political decision-making. However, critics argue the election will cement the power of President Tokayev, who has led the Central Asian country since 2019. Only seven state-approved parties, all described as loyal to Tokayev, were allowed to field candidates for the 145-seat parliament, while genuine opposition parties were banned. The constitutional changes also reset term limits, allowing Tokayev to run again in 2029. Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issetov stated that the election is part of a broader effort to modernize Kazakhstan’s political institutions and strengthen their ability to respond to the country’s changing social and economic landscape. He expects the new political system to help maintain stability, ensure further development of state institutions, provide more effective representation of public interests, and improve decision-making quality. The election takes place amid soaring inflation, hovering around 10.2 percent, and rising taxes. These economic conditions fuel concerns for the government of a repeat of the January 2022 cost-of-living unrest that resulted in 238 deaths among protesters and police. International observers monitored the electoral process, visiting polling stations and meeting with election officials and political parties.

title: Trump Rallies for Darline Graham in South Carolina; Protester Ejected
summary: President Trump held a rally for Darline Graham in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on Friday night. A protester interrupted Trump at approximately 7:28 p.m. and was escorted from the Myrtle Beach Convention Center by police and staff. The protester wore a black T-shirt reading, "Kill Your Local Pedophile." Trump paused his remarks, stating, "That person's going home to mom. Gonna get scolded because mom is voting for us." title: Iran Criticizes US Sanctions as 'Extraterritorial Sovereignty' Ahead of Announcement
summary: Iran maintains harsh rhetoric against US plans to impose tough new sanctions, with Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei stating on X on Saturday that the US declaration of new economic sanctions is an "assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent Member State of the United Nations." Baqaei added that such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will hold a news conference on Monday at 2 p.m. EDT (6 p.m. GMT) to detail the plan. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that the Trump administration's plan to crush Iran's economy will likely negate the need for major US military operations. He vowed the US will create "the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world" against Iran and stated to allies, "You are either with us or against us." President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday the "most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country" against Iran, threatening severe financial penalties on any nation that helps Tehran evade sanctions and calling it "Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale." Vice President JD Vance said economic pressure is the United States' "most effective tool" against Iran, noting Iran has felt "a lot more pressure than we have" in recent weeks. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf told an event in Baghdad on Friday that Muslim countries must plan to overcome "cruel" sanctions. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi rejected the US premise, stating Trump's campaign was "bound to fail" like previous rounds of US pressure. The war between the US and Iran neared six months old, with oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz virtually halted since the US launched its war against Iran on February 28. Iran threatens to strike unauthorized oil tankers attempting to transit the narrow waterway. title: Supreme Court Allows Trump White House Ballroom Construction to Continue
summary: The US Supreme Court allows construction on President Donald Trump's White House ballroom project to continue for now. Chief Justice John Roberts issued an administrative stay on Friday, temporarily blocking lower-court rulings that were set to halt above-ground construction. Roberts' one-page order will remain in effect until the Supreme Court takes further action and did not explain his reasoning or when the court would rule again. The order came just hours before lower-court rulings would have forced construction to stop. President Trump thanked the Supreme Court on Truth Social, stating, "We are grateful for the Decision of the United States Supreme Court." Trump called the project the "Military/Ballroom Complex" and said it is "so vital for National Security" and "will be THE GREATEST OF ITS KIND!" He also claimed presidents have sought such a facility for 150 years and the military for 100 years. Trump added that construction is "under budget and ahead of schedule." Administration lawyers argue the president has broad authority to make changes to federal properties and that the ballroom must be completed due to national security needs. Trump's lawyers described the East Wing ballroom as an "integrated military complex" needed to protect him, his staff, and guests from drones, terrorists, and snipers. They also stated the project is nearly two-thirds complete, at 65%, and involves material used in nuclear power plants that would be "virtually impossible to deconstruct." The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued in December, arguing Trump overstepped his authority by demolishing the East Wing in late 2025 without congressional approval. US District Judge Richard Leon agreed, ordering a stop to above-ground construction, though underground bunker work could proceed. The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed this order by a 2-1 vote on August 7 but paused its decision until Friday to allow an appeal to the Supreme Court. The ballroom is expected to be a 90,000-square-foot addition, projected to cost $400 million or more. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer criticized the Supreme Court's action, calling it "rubber stamping Trump's vanity-driven, gilded corruption."

The order temporarily blocks lower court rulings that would have halted above-ground construction of the ballroom.
President Trump thanked the Supreme Court for the decision, calling the project a "Military/Ballroom Complex" vital for national security.

title: Turkey Seeks Netanyahu Arrest Warrant, Accuses Him of 'Genocide'
summary: Turkey seeks an international arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of "genocide" linked to the interception of an aid flotilla bound for Gaza. Turkey's Justice Minister Akin Gurlek stated on X on Friday that his ministry requested the interior ministry issue Interpol Red Notices for Netanyahu and another suspect, Afek Moskovitch, so they may be sought internationally. Gurlek said arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Moskovitch were issued on July 14, 2026, as part of proceedings before Istanbul's 11th High Criminal Court. The charges include genocide, crimes against humanity, torture, deprivation of liberty, hijacking a transport vehicle, and property damage, stemming from an attack on the activist-operated Global Sumud Flotilla. Netanyahu's office responded on Friday night, calling Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan an "antisemitic dictator who has massacred Kurds, harbours Hamas terrorists, occupies half of Cyprus, and jails record numbers of journalists and politicians who oppose him." Netanyahu's office added that Erdogan "now seeks to extend his aggression against Israel into Syria" and that "Israel will not tolerate it." It also stated that "Erdogan's pathetic attempt to intimidate the leaders and soldiers of Israel, the only true democracy in the Middle East, will go nowhere." Turkey's presidential communications directorate described Netanyahu's comments as a "groundless rant" and a "cheap political ploy" aimed at gaining an advantage in the upcoming October legislative elections in Israel. The directorate stated that Netanyahu's administration is "awaiting accountability before international justice mechanisms on charges of genocide." Turkey has been a fierce critic of Israel's war in Gaza, which was sparked by the Hamas-led October 7 attacks on southern Israel. Turkish authorities accuse Netanyahu and Moskovitch of crimes against humanity, genocide, aggravated deprivation of liberty, intentional injury, torture, property damage, aggravated robbery, and hijacking of transportation vehicles in connection with the armed intervention against the flotilla and the detention of activists. Interpol reviews requests from member states before deciding whether to issue red notices.
