title: Imran Khan's Party Files Contempt Petition Over Hospital Transfer
summary: The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan filed a contempt petition against the government on Saturday. The petition seeks action against the prime minister, law minister, information minister, and other government officials for allegedly violating a Supreme Court order regarding Khan's hospital transfer. Naeem Panjutha, a legal adviser for Khan's PTI party, confirmed the filing. Khan's sister, Uzma Khan, also filed a separate petition in the Supreme Court, accusing the government and senior officials of "wilful, deliberate and contumacious disobedience" of the August 18 order. Eight members of the Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) on Saturday condemned the government's "blatant, wilful and deliberate violation" of the Supreme Court's August 18 order. They stated the executive has no authority to defy Supreme Court directions and that the actions constitute a "serious assault on the independence, authority and dignity of the judiciary." A three-judge Supreme Court bench on Tuesday, August 18, directed the government to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to the private Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad within two days for medical examination. The court also ordered Khan to remain at Shifa International Hospital until the next hearing on September 16. However, officials took Khan to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on Friday for a brief check-up before returning him to Adiala Jail. The government stated the medical evaluation at PIMS found no issue requiring immediate care. The PTI party interprets the court order as requiring Khan to remain under medical supervision until at least mid-September. Khan's family and party leaders termed the move a violation of the Supreme Court order. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Dr. Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said on Friday that the decision to move Khan to PIMS instead of Shifa was made by security agencies and was not political. He explained that security institutions assessed the situation and decided they could not control the law and order situation at Shifa. Khan's sister, Dr. Uzma Khan, stated after meeting her brother that he complained of being denied human interaction, suffering from anxiety, and fearing dying in isolation.

title: US Imposes 50% Tariffs on Canadian Goods; Canada Vows Matching Duties
summary: US tariffs of 50% on a wide array of Canadian goods took effect Saturday after last-minute trade talks collapsed Friday night. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada would impose reciprocal tariffs on US goods "dollar for dollar" to protect workers and businesses. The new tariffs impact nearly $20 billion (C$28 billion) worth of Canadian imports, or 5.5% of Canadian exports to the US, targeting products from hockey sticks to cement, electronics, industrial machinery, and dairy products. President Donald Trump had threatened a 50% levy on Canadian imports by August 19, temporarily pausing them earlier in the week, stating the two sides were close to a "very good" trade deal. Trade negotiators had been engaged in intense talks since July. Trump postponed the tariffs for three days on Tuesday, saying a deal had been reached. Canadian Minister Dominic LeBlanc and chief negotiator Janice Charette met with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington on Friday. Canada entered a technical recession in 2026 after two consecutive quarters of economic contraction. Roughly 70% of all Canadian exports head to the United States. Prime Minister Carney is diversifying Canada's trade by boosting exports outside the United States, heading to China, India, and Saudi Arabia. No further talks have been planned.

summary: Natalie Harp, 35, accompanied President Donald Trump to a Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, rally on Friday, a day after two fawning letters she wrote to him were revealed. title: Congo Receives 16,000 Ebola Vaccine Doses Amid Fastest Outbreak
summary: Congo received 16,250 doses of the Ervebo vaccine late Friday at N’djili International Airport in Kinshasa, as the country grapples with its fastest Ebola outbreak in history. Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba confirmed the arrival. The doses are the first of 70,000 expected from the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners, announced on Thursday. More doses are expected early next week. The current outbreak has recorded 2,557 deaths out of 5,375 confirmed cases across six affected provinces. The UN's senior Ebola coordinator, Julien Harneis, warned Friday that the outbreak is "growing exponentially" and spreading faster and wider than the response, covering an area larger than France. The outbreak, Congo's 17th, was officially declared May 15 but is believed to have been spreading for weeks beforehand. It is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is currently no approved treatment or vaccine. The Ervebo vaccine is licensed to treat the Zaire strain of Ebola, but early data from animal trials suggest it may offer some protection against Bundibugyo. Of the 70,000 doses, 20,000 will be used in a Phase 3 clinical trial to test its effect on the Bundibugyo strain, while 50,000 are allocated to frontline and health workers. The current outbreak is on track to surpass the deadliest outbreak on record, which killed over 11,000 people across West Africa between 2014 and 2016. Data from the Africa Centre for Disease Control shows transmission has not yet peaked and could reach three times its known rate. Efforts to contain the outbreak are hampered by armed conflict between the government and rebel groups, attacks on medical personnel and facilities, an itinerant labor population, displaced people, and a lack of critical infrastructure. Some frontline workers, like nurse Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo and hygiene worker Martin Bolombi, reported not being paid. WHO vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of Ervebo to see if it offered cross-protection against the Bundibugyo strain.

title: Karoline Leavitt Departs White House Press Secretary Role, Joins Super PAC

title: 18-Year-Old Kills One, Injures Three in Swedish High School Sword Attack
summary: Swedish police are investigating whether an 18-year-old man who attacked students at a high school in Fagersta with a sword on Friday, killing one, was involved in online communities promoting school violence. The attacker also severely injured two teenage boys before being arrested. The parents of a 17-year-old girl told Fagersta-Posten that their daughter was killed in the attack. Two boys, aged between 12 and 17, were seriously injured and admitted to hospital, with one undergoing emergency surgery, though both are in stable condition. A third person sustained lighter injuries. The attack occurred at Brinellskolan, which has about 400 to 500 students. Police received reports of the attack just after 2:00 pm (1200 GMT) on Friday. Officers shot the suspect during the arrest. Police are investigating a TikTok account that posted a picture of a sword 20 minutes before the assault, which appeared to be taken inside a school toilet. The month-old account contained videos referencing two mass violence attacks in Sweden and Norwegian far-right mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik, as well as a 2015 attack in Trollhattan. The Fagersta municipality stated that an assailant armed with a sword had entered Brinellskolan and wounded several people. Students, just back from summer holidays, were in lockdown at the school and several nearby schools for over three hours. Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson lamented the violence "right after the summer break" and canceled a speech scheduled for Saturday. King Carl XVI Gustaf expressed dismay and sadness. Police Chief Tommy Alriksson stated there was no reason to believe there were multiple perpetrators. Police are working to establish a motive and are interviewing many witnesses, which limits the information they can release.

title: Hong Kong Convicts Tiananmen Vigil Organizers of Inciting Subversion
summary: Hong Kong authorities hit back Saturday at "baseless slander and smearing" by Western countries over the convictions of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China and its former leaders for inciting subversion. A government spokesman stressed the High Court's "well-reasoned and sound" verdict. Former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung, 41, were found guilty on Friday of inciting subversion under a China-imposed national security law. A third defendant, former lawmaker Albert Ho, pleaded guilty when the trial opened in January. The alliance itself was also found guilty. The defendants could face up to 10 years in prison. Lee and Chow have been on remand for nearly five years since their September 2021 arrests. Ho has been behind bars since May 2021, except for a seven-month bail period. The Hong Kong Alliance, set up after the 1989 Tiananmen Square movement, organized annual June 4 vigils in Victoria Park and called for ending "one-party dictatorship" in mainland China. The three judges, in their 216-page judgment, found the alliance, Lee, and Chow incited public hatred towards the Communist Party of China by likening Beijing's 1989 crackdown to local authorities' response to the 2019 anti-government demonstrations. They ruled that any attempt to overthrow or undermine the party's leadership could constitute subversion because the country's constitution does not permit Western-style democracy. The government spokesman stated they were not prosecuted for their political beliefs, rejecting assertions by Western countries that the verdict demonstrated freedom of expression was being eroded. Hong Kong leader John Lee and Chief Superintendent Steve Li of the police’s National Security Department approved the convictions, with Lee stating the Alliance had "long been deliberately planting seeds of hatred against the CPC." Activists and overseas human rights groups expressed concern about declining freedoms in the city. The UK condemned the Chinese court's conviction. The sentencing for the convicted individuals has not yet been reported.

title: Trump Eases Beef Tariffs to Lower Prices, Faces Rancher Backlash
summary: President Donald Trump announced Friday that the United States will temporarily waive tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of additional beef imports for 90 days, a period lasting through the midterms. The move aims to ease consumer price strains. Trump stated that exporters agreed to a 25% discount below current market prices for this beef. Ground beef averaged $6.89 a pound. Beef prices have increased by almost 12% in the last year, and the American cattle herd has fallen to its lowest level in 75 years. Trump will formally sign an executive order on the tariff waiver for beef trimmings imports within the next two weeks. This push is cutting against pillars of Trump's economic agenda, including tariffs and favoring domestic producers. Trump previously signed an executive order in February 2026 increasing the amount of beef Argentina could export to the United States, citing the declining American cattle herd, the threat of New World screwworm, and persistent wildfires. He also directed the Justice Department to investigate meat packing companies over alleged collusion to drive up prices. The administration is under mounting pressure to deliver relief as affordability becomes a bigger political liability ahead of the midterms. US cattle producers and some Republican senators blasted the move, warning that cheaper imports could hurt ranchers and efforts to rebuild their depleted herds. The National Cattlemen's Beef Association president Colin Woodall stated, "You don't put America first by putting U.S. cattle producers last." Senator Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., advised President Trump against this action for a year, saying it would further harm American ranchers, "most of whom are MAGA Republicans." Senator Deb Fischer, R-Neb., expressed extreme disappointment, stating that flooding the market with foreign beef hurts the livestock industry and undermines the long-term solution of growing the US cattle herd. Trump defended his decision, saying it’s "what people want" and that "we want to get the beef prices down, so we will get them down a little bit." Trump did not specify which foreign beef exporters he had reached a deal with or which companies made commitments for the 25% discount.

title: US Judge Strikes Down Trump Visa Ban Affecting 75 Nations
summary: A United States District Court in Manhattan nullified the Donald Trump administration's policy suspending immigrant visa processing for 75 countries. U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas delivered the ruling on Friday, describing the January directive by the State Department as "patently unlawful" and exceeding the statutory authority of Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The policy, which took effect on January 21, had barred immigrant visa issuance to nationals of 75 countries, including Nigeria, on grounds they posed "a high risk for becoming a public charge." The directive stated that older or overweight applicants could be denied, along with those with past use of government cash assistance or institutionalization. Judge Vargas, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, held that the suspension ran afoul of federal immigration law, which expressly removed authority over consular processing of immigrant visas from the Secretary of State. The ruling reverses any visa denial based solely on this policy, potentially requiring review of thousands of old visa applications. The 75 affected countries are primarily non-European with non-white populations, spanning Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean, Eastern Europe, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East. Plaintiffs in the lawsuit included six US citizens whose relatives in Ghana, Jamaica, Guatemala, and Ethiopia were denied visas. Five professionals from Colombia, including an engineer, an architect, and a Harvard-trained endocrinologist, also had their visa applications denied under the policy. Immigrant rights groups Catholic Legal Immigration Network and African Communities Together filed the lawsuit, along with visa applicants and US citizens sponsoring family members. President Donald Trump had published a list of welfare dependent rates among immigrants, noting that about 33.3 percent of Nigeria immigrant households received some form of public assistance. President Trump has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown, which he says is aimed at improving domestic security. Rights groups say the crackdown has violated free speech and due process rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling. In 2018, the Supreme Court upheld the third iteration of Trump's travel ban, which restricted entry into the US by foreign nationals from several Muslim-majority countries.

title: Prince Harry, Elton John Ordered to Pay Millions in Failed Lawsuit
summary: Prince Harry, Elton John, and five other claimants have been ordered to pay an initial 9.5 million pounds ($13 million) to Associated Newspapers Ltd, publisher of the Daily Mail, following their failed invasion of privacy case. Justice Matthew Nicklin ruled on Friday that the payment must be made by August 28. The payment is at the upper end of expectations and marks a vindication for the Daily Mail journalists. The claimants could face an additional liability of around 25 million pounds in legal costs if the publisher seeks to recover the remaining amount and receives legal approval. Associated Newspapers stated it spent over 34 million pounds in costs during the case. The high-profile claimants lost their High Court case in London last month, where they accused Associated Newspapers of alleged wrongdoing, including unlawful phone hacking. Other claimants include anti-racism campaigner Doreen Lawrence, whose son Stephen was murdered in 1993; Elton John's husband and film producer David Furnish; actors Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley; and politician Simon Hughes. Lawrence's legal costs are expected to be covered by the other claimants. Justice Nicklin criticized the claims as "speculative" and "substantially inferential," adding they "lacked a proper evidential foundation." He also noted "several features" influenced his decision, including the claimants' failure to "voluntarily" withdraw serious allegations that could no longer be supported. Justice Nicklin stated the conduct was "unreasonable to a high degree." The judge ruled that Associated Newspapers' costs should be determined on an indemnity basis, a move the publisher had pushed for. Lawyers for the claimants had urged the interim payment be set at around 7.9 million pounds (€9.2 million), while Associated Newspapers had asked for approximately 9.9 million pounds (€11.6 million). The claimants reportedly had insurance covering roughly half the initial budget estimates provided by Associated Newspapers' lawyers. The High Court heard the charges during an 11-week trial earlier this year, which concluded last month with the judge dismissing all cases.

title: TikTok Agrees to $400 Million Settlement in US Children's Privacy Case
summary: TikTok has agreed to pay $400 million to settle a lawsuit with the US Department of Justice (DOJ) over alleged violations of children's online privacy laws. The DOJ announced the settlement on Friday. The settlement is one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a case under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly. The DOJ and Federal Trade Commission (FTC) sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance in August 2024 during former President Joe Biden's administration. The lawsuit alleged that TikTok failed to protect children's privacy and illegally collected their information, including names and email addresses, without parental consent for users under 13. The case dates back to 2019 when the US filed a COPPA lawsuit against Musical.ly, which ByteDance bought in 2017 and merged into TikTok. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. called the settlement a "major victory for American children and parents." The DOJ stated that since the lawsuit was filed, TikTok has undergone " changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions, and privacy practices." The company has implemented "extensive measures designed to strengthen safeguards for younger users, improve age-related controls, and enhance parental oversight." In 2024, Biden had pushed for TikTok to be banned or forced to sell its US operations, which happened last year with Donald Trump's support. TikTok's US operations are now 81% owned by a consortium of investors, while ByteDance maintains a 19% stake. The lawsuit alleged that even accounts created in a "Kids Mode" designed for users under 13 had collected email addresses and other personal information. The settlement resolves the allegations without TikTok admitting wrongdoing or facing further litigation. The same COPPA legislation is currently being used by 29 states to sue Meta for misusing children's data, with Meta denying the allegations.

title: Pentagon Fires Stars and Stripes Editor, Publisher, Reporter for Insubordination
summary: The Defense Department fired Erik Slavin, the editor-in-chief, and Max Lederer, the publisher, of Stars and Stripes on Friday. Lara Korte, a Middle East correspondent at the news outlet, was also fired. The Pentagon sent termination notices to Slavin and Lederer, who had announced his retirement earlier this week, citing conflict with Pentagon leadership on the paper's direction. Slavin's termination notice cited insubordination and an unauthorized media appearance as reasons for his dismissal. In July, CBS News interviewed Slavin and Korte for a segment on accusations of editorial interference at Stars and Stripes. Slavin stated he was fired for saying in a CBS interview that "hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a personal red line." Korte said on social media she was fired for insubordination "after I told a CBS reporter that I work for Stars and Stripes, not the Pentagon, not any administration, and not any policy maker." Lederer, who served as publisher since 2007, had announced his intention to retire in September, stating it was clear the Pentagon had a new vision for the newspaper that differed from his own. The firings raised questions about the Pentagon's willingness to ensure the editorial integrity of the publication. Stars and Stripes, a government-funded news outlet, reports on the U.S. military and has published continuously since World War Two, historically maintaining editorial independence. The terminations came about 10 days after Stars and Stripes journalists reported on hardships faced by Navy sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose deployment was extended to nine months amid the war in Iran. The Pentagon recently appointed Navy Captain William Urban, an active duty serviceman, as the outlet's military deputy to the publisher without Lederer's prior knowledge. Captain Urban stated in a letter published Friday that his priority was to ensure "the highest quality of editorially independent reporting" at Stars and Stripes. US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has been critical of the media since taking office in 2025.

title: Data Center Backlash Grows; Politicians Shift Stances Amid Midterm Races
summary: Tech leaders are debating the reasons for widespread public opposition to data centers, with some suggesting public ignorance or foreign influence. title: Trump Claims Iran Not Ready For "Right Deal" After Economic D-Day Threat

title: European Wildfires Expose, Detonate Buried World War Bombs

title: South Korea Launches First Arctic Commercial Shipping Voyage to Europe
summary: A South Korean container ship, the PanStar Acro, sets sail on Saturday for Europe via the Arctic, marking the nation's first commercial voyage on the route. President Lee Jae Myung has made Arctic shipping a priority for South Korea, with officials aiming to transform the port of Busan into a global maritime hub and establish the Arctic as a regular trade route by 2030. The PanStar Acro has secured 837 TEU of cargo, including auto parts and chemical products. India is also preparing to dispatch its first cargo ship along the same corridor next year, as stated by S. Venkatesapathy, a joint secretary in India’s shipping ministry, on August 13. Two crises are driving Asian shippers north: climate change, which has opened a navigable window from July to October due to melting ice, and geopolitics, with threats to shipping in the Red Sea and the near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war. The Northern Sea Route promises to reduce transit times between Asia and northern Europe by approximately two weeks, shortening shipping distances by up to 40 percent compared to the Suez Canal route. Russian President Vladimir Putin held a special meeting of the Russian Security Council on Friday to discuss securing and developing Russia’s assets in the Arctic Circle. Last year, 88 vessels made 103 transits through the route, an increase from 97 in 2024 and 43 in 2022.

title: Pentagon Reports Increased Sexual Assault Reporting, Decreased Incidents Among Troops

title: Longer-Dated Treasury Yields Rise Despite Bessent's Bond Buyback Increase
summary: Longer-dated Treasury yields rose this week, with 30-year Treasury yields reaching their highest level since 2007. On August 18, a widespread global selloff of U.S. Treasury securities pushed 30-year yields to roughly 5.34%. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent responded on Wednesday by doubling bond buybacks from $2 billion to $4 billion, starting next month. This move is a routine operation begun in 2024 to provide a market for longer-dated debt. Bessent insisted the action was not an attempt to tamp down yields. The buyback announcement briefly lowered yields, but they rebounded Thursday and were up again Friday, erasing Wednesday's declines. Investors over the past several days priced in a likelihood of higher inflation, with the breakeven rate, a market-based measure comparing Treasury yields to inflation-protected securities, rising across the curve to its highest level in over two months. The 10-year breakeven rate rose to 2.34% on Thursday, its highest since June 10, and five-year breakevens hit the same level, highest since June 16. Economists worry the Treasury Department’s bond buying could put more pressure on the Federal Reserve to curb inflation. Minutes released this week from the last Federal Open Market Committee meeting stated that "risks to the inflation forecast were seen as skewed to the upside," with some participants noting large price increases from artificial intelligence data centers. The Fed voted 9-3 at its last meeting to hold interest rates at 3.5% to 3.75% and meets again on September 15. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is scheduled to speak at the annual Jackson Hole Symposium next week. Van Hesser, chief strategist at KBRA, a credit and bond rating agency, cited a "cocktail of concerns" in the market. Oil prices also rose for a second straight week as U.S.-Iran peace talks stalled, and Bessent threatened "toughest sanctions in history" against Iran. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 454 points for the week, the S&P 500 fell 111 points, and the Nasdaq dropped 549 points.

title: Treasury Secretary Bessent Vows Bigger Buybacks After Debt Hits $40 Trillion
summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated on Thursday that the Treasury will increase the size of its debt buybacks, less than 24 hours after doubling them. Bessent clarified that Wednesday's $4 billion ceiling per operation is a floor, not a strict limit, and that buybacks "could be more than the $4 billion per issue." He attributed the move to signaling that yields do not reflect underlying fundamentals and to address weak liquidity at the 30-year point. The 30-year yield is trading at 5.25% after hitting 5.33% on Tuesday, and the 10-year yield is at 4.7% after topping 4.75% on the same day. The US gross national debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time on Tuesday, according to Treasury Department data released Wednesday. This figure includes $32 trillion owed to investors and other outside holders, with the remainder owed to government accounts. The debt has grown by $3 trillion in the past year alone and has doubled since January 2017, when it stood at roughly $20 trillion. The Congressional Budget Office projects a deficit of approximately $2.1 trillion for this fiscal year, with the Treasury needing to refinance $9.7 trillion in debt coming due. title: Hong Kong Court Convicts Tiananmen Vigil Organizers of Inciting Subversion
summary: Two Hong Kong activists, Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, were found guilty of "incitement to subversion" on Friday, August 21. The conviction falls under Beijing's national security law, imposed in 2020. A press summary states they "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power." Each faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in jail, with sentencing to be determined later. The trial for Lee and Chow began in January and spanned 24 days. A third defendant, 74-year-old former lawmaker Albert Ho, pleaded guilty in January. Chow, who represented herself, told the court in May that the law itself was on trial. The court ruling stated that Lee, Chow, and Ho "had all along been hostile" toward China's ruling Communist Party and the central government. Judges determined they "intentionally encouraged supporters of the alliance to wait for the right time to carry out the goal of 'end one-party dictatorship' with unlawful means." Lee's wife, Elizabeth Tang, described the judgment as unjust and absurd, noting an absence of evidence for illegal means. Taiwan called on China to "stop political persecution" and immediately release those detained in the case. The Hong Kong Alliance was founded in May 1989 to support pro-democracy rallies, and authorities banned its annual gatherings in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, with vigils never resuming.

title: Russia Warns UK of Consequences Over Drone Partnership with Ukraine
summary: The Kremlin has often issued threats that Britain will "pay a higher price" for its role in Ukraine, as it did again this week following reports of British-made drones striking deep inside Russian territory. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, renewed threats on Tuesday, August 2026, of a strike on the UK for supplying long-range drones to Kyiv. Lavrov spoke of "consequences," and Kremlin propagandists urged Russian people to support actions up to a nuclear strike. Katia Glod, deputy head of foreign policy at the New Eurasia Strategies Centre (NEST) think tank, stated Putin's threats should be taken seriously but not toward a "real, kinetic move against Britain" in terms of war. Glod emphasized that direct strikes on the UK would be "playing with fire" due to NATO's mutual defense agreement. Putin knows Russia "doesn't have the capacity to respond" to a NATO response. The UK-Ukraine drone partnership aims to boost long-term security. The UK allowed Ukraine to use British-supplied Storm Shadow cruise missiles against targets inside Russia in late 2024, leading to Moscow's accusations of escalation and threats. Long-range drones are cheaper and easier to manufacture than Storm Shadow missiles, allowing for a potential "cumulative effect of repeated mass strikes deep inside Russia." The UK has a substantial uncrewed-systems sector, including drone programs like Nyan, AR3, K3 Scout, and Octopus. The Uncrewed Systems Centre in Swindon is described by the government as Europe's "largest drone testing center." US intelligence warned Putin was planning to attack a Baltic state or Poland in the "coming months," prompting a snap NATO drill with 50 military aircraft in the Baltic Sea on Wednesday, August 20. title: USS Abraham Lincoln Departs Middle East After Nine-Month Deployment

The USS George Washington arrived in the Middle East on Wednesday to begin a deployment, replacing the Lincoln. U.S. Central Command's commander, Adm. Brad Cooper, announced the Lincoln's return home to its crew on Saturday. The Lincoln, with roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines, has been at sea for more than 250 days. The deployment began on November 21, 2025, from San Diego. The war with Iran, which began in February, extended the mission and intensified the workload. title: Navy Considers Renaming Carrier USS Doris Miller After Trump
summary: Navy leadership is discussing renaming a future aircraft carrier after President Donald Trump instead of a heroic Black service member, according to two U.S. officials. The ship, designated CVN-81, is currently set to be named the USS Doris Miller, honoring an enlisted sailor who shot down at least one Japanese plane and helped carry wounded Americans to safety during the attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Doris Miller was the first Black sailor awarded the Navy Cross in May 1942. The decision to name the Ford-class carrier after Miller was made in 2020 during Trump's first term, marking the first time a U.S. aircraft carrier would be named after an enlisted sailor and the first named after a Black American. Discussions about changing the name have been ongoing for several months, and the Navy has stopped internally referring to the ship as the USS Doris Miller. Thomas Bledsoe, Doris Miller's great-nephew, relayed the family's shock and concerns, stating they were not informed of the potential change. The Navy is reportedly considering renaming another warship after Miller and recommending him for the Medal of Honor, the highest decoration for military valor, which requires final authorization from Congress and approval from Trump. Ship-naming authority rests with the Navy secretary, but defense secretaries are often deeply involved, meaning the decision will be made by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao. Naming an aircraft carrier after a sitting president would be an unprecedented move. Rep. Jason Crow (D-CO) criticized the potential renaming. The Pentagon and a Department of Defense spokesperson stated they have nothing to announce at this time. Trump also ordered the USS Doris Miller to rip out its electromagnetic catapults in favor of steam-powered systems, and the ship could be among the first to have this Trump-ordered system.

title: Seven Nations Demand Israel Halt West Bank Settlement Plan
summary: The Netherlands, Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, and Norway have jointly condemned Israel's decision to open bidding on a major settlement project in the occupied West Bank. title: Angie Nixon Wins Florida Democratic Senate Primary in Upset
summary: State Representative Angie Nixon (D) won the Florida Democratic U.S. Senate primary on Tuesday, defeating Alexander Vindman. title: US National Debt Tops $40 Trillion, Treasury Doubles Bond Buybacks
summary: The U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion on Tuesday, according to Treasury Department data. This milestone follows the debt reaching $39 trillion in March and $38 trillion in October 2025. The Treasury Department responded to bond market pressure by pledging to double its buybacks of older securities. Starting September 9, the maximum size of each buyback operation in the 10-to-20-year and 20-to-30-year markets will increase from $2 billion to $4 billion, continuing through November 4. This decision came as the 30-year yield climbed to its highest level since 2007 on Tuesday, reaching 5.3%. President Donald Trump stated, "No, I don't think so," when asked if Americans should worry about the volatility. The gross national debt, which includes intragovernmental accounts like Social Security trust funds, has more than doubled from $19.9 trillion since President Trump's first term began on January 20, 2017. The debt held by the public, a separate metric, is currently over $32 trillion. Interest expenses from servicing the national debt now exceed $1 trillion per year. The budget deficit is expected to surpass $2 trillion this year, or nearly 6% of GDP. Factors contributing to the debt's growth include increased enrollment in Social Security and Medicare, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, massive spending on COVID-19 relief measures, and increased government spending due to the war with Iran. Revenues have fallen due to tariff refunds and tax cuts for businesses and wealthy individuals from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. White House spokesman Kush Desai stated the Trump administration focuses on "slashing waste, fraud, and abuse in government spending to accelerating economic growth and getting America's debt-to-GDP ratio back on the right track." Michael Peterson, CEO of the nonpartisan Peter G. Peterson Foundation, told CBS News that the government has ignored structural challenges in the budget, causing the debt problem to worsen.

title: Moderna, Merck mRNA Vaccine Shows Promise in Late-Stage Melanoma Trial
summary: Moderna and Merck reported positive late-stage trial results for their personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, intismeran autogene, when used with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda (pembrolizumab). The Phase 3 trial found the combination met its main goal of recurrence-free survival and a key secondary endpoint of distant metastasis-free survival. The vaccine, combined with Keytruda, reduced the recurrence of melanoma in a large, late-stage trial and also slowed the spread to new areas of the body, the companies said. This study marks the first positive final-stage trial for any mRNA-based cancer therapy. The trial involved over 1,100 people whose melanoma was in advanced stages, with patients having visible signs of their tumors surgically removed before the trial. The vaccine is personalized, built from a patient's own tumor, which has its own genetic sequence. Artificial intelligence helps identify unique mutations for inclusion in the vaccine. The mRNA delivers synthetic mRNA into cells, training the immune system to attack cancer cells, while Keytruda removes a "cloak of invisibility" from cancer cells, according to Dr. Jon LaPook. Moderna shares spiked by a record 177 percent on Wednesday, and Merck shares climbed nearly 13 percent. Moderna president Stephen Hoge stated the product could be approved by regulators as soon as 2027. Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, called it an "auspicious start." Jedd Wolchok, a melanoma expert and director of the Meyer Cancer Centre at Weill Cornell Medicine, described it as an important step forward for cancer immunotherapy and vaccines. Earlier Phase 2b trial results showed the vaccine/Keytruda combination reduced the risk of cancer recurrence or death by 49 percent compared to Keytruda alone. The companies did not release specific efficacy numbers for the Phase 3 trial, stating they will be shared at an upcoming medical meeting and with regulators. The trial is still underway to see if patients who receive the vaccine live longer. Melanoma is the most serious form of skin cancer. Roughly 112,000 people are diagnosed with melanoma in the US each year, and about 8,500 die from it, according to the American Cancer Society.

summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) has condemned U.S. sanctions against its President Tomoko Akane of Japan and trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, calling the move a "flagrant attack" on the court's independence. The ICC stated the sanctions "undermine the rule of law" and jeopardize the international legal order. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa stated they "stand firmly" with the court. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres voiced "serious concern" and UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk urged Washington to lift the sanctions. The U.S. sanctions are part of a broader pressure campaign against the ICC, which issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza. summary: The Supreme Court (SC) of Pakistan returned a review petition filed by the federal government challenging its August 18 order to shift incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan to Shifa International Hospital. title: Prime Minister Burnham Pledges to End Rough Sleeping by Christmas
summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham unveiled plans on August 19 to offer those sleeping rough a way off the streets by Christmas. Burnham pledged to donate 15 percent of his £180,000 annual salary to homelessness causes. His government will provide emergency accommodation and long-term housing support across England this winter. The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government later clarified the pledge refers to both short and long-term rough sleeping. The MHCLG also stated it will only be measuring rough sleeping in England, acknowledging devolved nations are responsible for their own policies. summary: President Donald Trump showcased the ongoing construction of a multimillion-dollar granite helipad and a new ballroom at the White House on Wednesday, inviting the press for a tour. title: UK Threatens Sanctions Over Israeli West Bank Settlement Expansion
summary: UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband condemned Israel's publication of a tender for the E1 settlement project in the West Bank on Wednesday, calling it an "unacceptable and destructive act." Miliband stated the project risks separating the West Bank from East Jerusalem, endangering the viability of a two-state solution, and constitutes a "flagrant breach of international law." The E1 project involves marketing the first 1,400 housing units, part of a larger plan for 3,412 homes between Jerusalem and Ma'aleh Adumim. The Civil Administration's Higher Planning Committee approved the project in August 2025. Plans to build in the E1 area have been under consideration for over two decades and are internationally condemned. title: Manipur Shuts Schools Amid Protests Demanding NRC Before Census
summary: The Manipur government ordered the closure of all educational institutions for three days, from August 20 to August 22, citing the "prevailing law-and-order situation." This decision follows intensified large-scale protests demanding the implementation of the National Register of Citizens (NRC) with 1951 as the base year, before the Census exercise. The Campaign for Just and Fair Delimitation (JFD) and local civil society groups escalated their agitation as the government scheduled training sessions for census workers, leading to the cancellation of these sessions in several valley districts. During the protests, bandh supporters burnt effigies of Chief Minister Y Khemchand Singh and Home Minister Govindas Konthoujam at Khurai Lamlong in Imphal East district. Market places, educational institutions, and public transport were affected in five valley districts, including Imphal West, Imphal East, Kakching, Thoubal, and Bishnupur. The house-listing phase of Census 2027 in Manipur is scheduled to run from September 1 to September 30. The United Naga Council also reiterated its demand to defer the Census and delimitation until NRC implementation. title: Missing Australian Hiker Lily Hooper Found Dead After Eight-Day Search
summary: The body of 18-year-old Australian hiker Lily Hooper was found dead in Nattai National Park on Thursday, eight days after she vanished during a solo trip. title: Donalds, Jolly Win Florida Governor Primaries, Set For Debates
summary: Representative Byron Donalds (R-FL) won the Republican primary for Florida governor on Tuesday, and former Representative David Jolly won the Democratic primary, setting up their general election contest to succeed Governor Ron DeSantis. Donalds, who is backed by Trump, challenged his Democrat opponent, David Jolly, to three debates on Wednesday. Donalds labeled Jolly a "Trojan horse" for "Democrat socialists" and criticized his policy positions, including government-run property insurance. He also criticized "Democrat policy" for rising healthcare costs and inflation, attributing struggles to such policies. The Associated Press called the race for Donalds at 8 p.m. EDT on Tuesday. With 83% of the vote counted, Donalds had secured 48.7%, or 715,409 votes. Donalds defeated 10 other Republicans for the GOP gubernatorial nomination. Both Donalds and Jolly are described as pro-Israel candidates. Jolly had previously responded to Donalds' debate challenge by saying, "Get through your primary, and we'll talk." title: Many Fed Officials See Need for Higher Rates if Inflation Persists
summary: Multiple Federal Reserve officials indicated the central bank may need to raise interest rates later this year, according to newly released minutes of the Fed’s July meeting. The minutes from the July 28-29 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and the Fed’s Board of Governors showed that "many" participants assessed that policy tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline. Officials voted 9-3 at the meeting to keep their key rate unchanged at about 3.6%, targeted in a range between 3.5%-3.75%. The three dissenting votes were regional presidents Beth Hammack of Cleveland, Lorie Logan of Dallas, and Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis, who favored a quarter percentage point increase. Fed officials were heavily focused on the threat of stubbornly elevated inflation, worrying that the Iran war, tariffs, and heavy investment in AI infrastructure were boosting prices. They judged their inflation outlooks as highly uncertain and inflation risks skewed to the upside. Since the July meeting, inflation data has been generally positive, though the annual rate remains well above the Fed's 2% target. The U.S. economy grew at a 1.5% annualized rate in the second quarter. President Donald Trump expressed frustration on Wednesday that the Federal Reserve is not cutting interest rates, accusing Fed officials of political motives, though he excluded Chairman Kevin Warsh. Trump argued rate cuts are needed to keep the economy growing and reduce the financing burden of the nation's nearly $40 trillion debt. Wall Street investors now expect the Fed to remain on hold at its next meeting in September and potentially lift rates in December, though that outlook could change.

title: Prosecutors Seek Life Without Parole for Australian Mushroom Murderer Erin Patterson

title: Study Finds European Wildfire Area Could Nearly Triple by Century's End
summary: New research finds that wildfires could burn nearly three times as much of Europe each year by the end of the century. A study published Thursday by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) concludes that under a high-emissions pathway, the annual burned area in Europe could rise by approximately 192 percent. Researchers arrived at these figures by comparing projected averages for 2070-2100 against a modeled 2000-2030 baseline. They ran two separate fire models across five climate projections. Maik Billing, a PIK researcher and lead author of the study, stated that "climate change is driving up fire activity across Europe as hot, dry and windy conditions become more severe." He added that if global temperatures rise by approximately 3.6°C, fires would become "much more prevalent," including in areas that have not experienced many fires to date, such as western Germany and the Netherlands. The study projects the Mediterranean region would be the worst hit, with other local wildfire hotspots likely to emerge in the foothills of mountainous areas like the Alps, Pyrenees, and Carpathians. A second modeling effort, developed by co-authors from the Senckenberg institute, suggests that human prevention efforts could reduce burned areas. Improvements in prevention, detection, and firefighting could reduce the burned area by 92 percent in a world with 1.8°C warming and by 72 percent in a world that is 3.6°C hotter. Senckenberg scientist Thomas Hickler stated, "We need to invest more." The warning follows weeks of devastating wildfires across Europe this summer, fueled by dry conditions and a historically hot summer. Over 600,000 hectares have burned so far this fire season, which is set to become the third-worst on record for the EU, behind 2025 and 2022.

summary: Portugal's President António Jose Seguro has enacted a law banning face coverings in public spaces, a measure widely seen as targeting Muslim women who wear full-face veils. This development follows the expiration on Monday of a 60-day negotiation period agreed to in a June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran. President Trump also threatened to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way" of a deal with Iran on Hormuz, according to Fox News. Iran has kept control of the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, requiring vessels to seek permission and pay transit service fees. The U.S. is also blockading Iranian shipping traffic through the strait. title: Florida State Representative Angie Nixon Wins Democratic Senate Primary
summary: Florida state Representative Angie Nixon defeated Alex Vindman in the Democratic U.S. Senate primary, securing 56 percent of the vote to Vindman's 44 percent. summary: US President Donald Trump announced a three-day pause on 50 percent tariffs against Canadian imports, citing a tentative trade deal. title: Chinese Humanoid Robot Maker Unitree Shares Soar in Shanghai Debut
summary: Unitree Robotics, a Chinese humanoid robot maker, made its stock market debut in Shanghai on Wednesday, with its shares ending the first day of trading up by more than 460%. The company's shares, initially offered at 150.80 yuan ($22.36) each, closed at 845 yuan ($125.40). Earlier in the day, shares went as high as 1,100 yuan ($163.23), a 629% increase. title: Philippine Student Kills Classmate, Himself in Livestreamed School Attack
summary: Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla announced on Wednesday that the child involved in the Ateneo de Zamboanga University (AdZU) shooting was driven onto campus in his father's private vehicle, bypassing standard security checks. The shooting incident occurred on Tuesday morning, August 18, at the junior high school building of AdZU’s Tumaga campus in Zamboanga City. Remulla, citing police reports, confirmed two fatalities: the student gunman and a Grade 10 student. Two other students were injured: a female grazed on her back and a male who fainted. The suspect, identified by police as Grade 9 student Mohammad Mael Jalani, fired at a teacher but apparently missed, then shot a Grade 10 student on the fourth floor before going up one floor and killing himself. Zamboanga city Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso and police said the suspect shot himself. The student livestreamed the attack on social media using a body-worn camera, with snippets appearing on Facebook Live. His Facebook account has since been disabled. Authorities recovered two firearms, a.40-caliber and a 9mm-caliber, along with "voluminous ammunition," including two live 9mm rounds, five live.40-caliber rounds, four fired 9mm cartridges, and three fired.40-caliber cartridges. The firearms belonged to the student's father, a uniformed police officer from the Bureau of Customs. Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno ordered the preventive suspension of the shooter’s father on August 18. The father claimed he left his gun bag in his vehicle, where the student retrieved it, but Remulla expressed skepticism, citing police training on gun safety. Education Secretary Sonny Angara denied widely shared speculations that the student gunman was bullied or depressed, stating his motive remains a "mystery." Angara said investigators cannot yet determine whom the student specifically sought to target, noting he entered two classrooms but fired only in the second. This incident marks the second fatal school shooting in the Philippines in two months, following one in Tacloban City in June. The October before that, a shooting occurred in Marikina. title: DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Surpasses 5,000 Cases; WHO Declares Global Emergency
summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reached 5,000 cases, with government data showing 5,021 cases and 2,378 deaths as of Sunday. World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Tuesday the outbreak remains a global health emergency and is "far from being under control." Ghebreyesus stated the outbreak is spreading faster than any previous one in the country and the risk of national and international spread remains high. The current outbreak, which began in mid-May, has infected and killed more people at a greater speed than any other in history. It is Congo's 17th Ebola epidemic and has become the deadliest in the country's history, surpassing the 2018-2020 outbreak. The WHO estimates it will likely surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak, which recorded over 11,000 deaths. Dieudonne Mwamba, Director General of the DRC’s National Public Health Institute, noted an increase in cases and deaths in recent weeks, attributing it to unsafe areas and community resistance fueled by misinformation. The outbreak has spread to six provinces in the north and east, regions characterized by weak state presence, lacking health infrastructure, and ongoing conflict with armed groups. Mwamba called for combined efforts to contain the epidemic, starting with Ituri Province, its epicenter. Thérèse Anyiya, a nurse in Ituri's capital Bunia, expressed exhaustion due to work demands and poor conditions, noting some health workers have gone on strike over unpaid wages. Attacks on medical teams and vehicles are a recurring challenge, with one ambulance attacked in Bunia, according to Dr. Thierno Baldé, a WHO incident manager. Residents attacked a health team on Monday in Aru territory after a suspected case, setting fire to an ambulance and damaging two other vehicles. The ongoing outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which has no approved vaccines or treatments. The WHO emergency committee held its second meeting on Tuesday since declaring the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on May 17. Ghebreyesus urged international assistance and said new recommendations would be issued to DRC and other at-risk countries.

title: Trump Labels Strait of Hormuz 'New US Territory'; Iran Denounces Claim
summary: The Trump administration indicates it favors economic warfare in its approach to the conflict with Iran, touting its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and previewing new sanctions. President Donald Trump told Fox News on Monday he is "not in a hurry" for a solution, suggesting a longer-term squeeze. A 60-day memorandum of understanding (MoU) between the U.S. and Iran to lay groundwork for peace expired on Monday, with no replacement agreement. Kpler data reported 28 vessels transited in a three-day period between Friday and Sunday. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz slowed on August 19, with Kpler data showing six commodity vessels crossed on August 18, down from nine a day earlier and below the 10-day daily average of 11. On Tuesday, President Trump posted a map on Truth Social labeling the Strait of Hormuz "New U.S. Territory," echoing a claim he first floated last week. Ghalibaf said on Tuesday the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the U.S. lifts its blockade, releases Iran's frozen assets, and removes sanctions. title: Australian Woman Erin Patterson Appeals Murder Convictions in Mushroom Poisoning Case
summary: Convicted Australian triple-murderer Erin Patterson appealed her convictions Wednesday for poisoning four of her estranged husband's relatives with death cap mushrooms. Three judges of the Victoria state Court of Appeal are hearing her appeal over two days. Patterson's defense attorney, Richard Edney, presented the first ground for appeal: an error that resulted in jury members being sequestered in the same hotel as a police witness and members of the prosecution team. Edney called this a "very serious breach of sequestration" and "catastrophic." Prosecutors, meanwhile, are appealing Patterson's sentence, arguing it was too lenient. Patterson was sentenced in September last year to life in prison, with a non-parole period of 33 years. Prosecutors will argue Thursday that she should be sentenced to life without the possibility of parole. Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane said there was no evidence of actual contact between any juror and any other person. Kissane accepted the hotel arrangement was regrettable but happened "by accident." Patterson was found guilty last July of three counts of murder and one of attempted murder. The charges relate to a lunch of beef Wellington pastries she prepared at her rural home in Leongatha, southeast Australia, in July 2023. Her victims include her estranged husband's parents, Don and Gail Patterson, both 70, and Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson, 66. Heather's husband, Ian Wilkinson, was the only surviving guest. Another defense lawyer, Veronika Drago, argued there was no evidence Patterson had read online posts reporting death cap mushrooms near Loch and Outtrim. The trial heard evidence from a telecommunications expert that Patterson's phone connected to towers near those towns. Prosecutor Jeremy McWilliams said this evidence showed Patterson had an opportunity to deliberately source death cap mushrooms. Patterson, 51, watched the appeal hearing via video link from prison.

summary: Meta is facing a massive legal challenge in the United States, with 29 states seeking remedies that could expose the company to as much as $1.4 trillion. The lawsuit, being heard in Oakland, California, accuses Meta of designing Facebook and Instagram features like infinite scrolling, autoplay, and algorithm-driven recommendations to keep young users engaged. A bipartisan group of 29 US states is suing Meta, seeking potentially tens or hundreds of billions of dollars in penalties and changes to how Meta conducts business. summary: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) announced it had paused all trade and financial transactions with Iran after reporting that two ballistic missiles were launched from Iran toward its territorial waters. title: Trump Pauses 50% Tariffs on Canadian Goods for Three Days

title: Kushner Warns Hamas: Disarm Gaza or Face Israeli Military Action
summary: US special envoy Jared Kushner stated on Monday that Hamas must honor its commitments to disarm or face an Israeli Defense Force (IDF) operation to “finish the job.” Kushner told FOX News's Trey Yingst that if Hamas fails to follow through, Israel will have “a lot more support from the US and others.” His comments followed meetings with Hamas and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) in Cairo on Sunday, and with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog in Jerusalem on Monday. Hamas affirmed its “commitment” to Trump's 20-point peace plan and a “15-point roadmap” where they commit to “giving up their weapons.” Kushner described the meeting with Hamas as “cordial,” stating they “said all the right things,” but acknowledged it is “very, very hard to trust” a terrorist organization. Kushner indicated that progress on demilitarization could begin in “as little as 30 days,” with weapons removal and tunnel filling in “60 to 90 days.” He stated that the US would not support rebuilding Gaza before demilitarization occurs. Kushner met with Netanyahu for nearly four hours, describing it as “very, very good” and addressing “valid concerns” raised by the Israeli prime minister. Netanyahu had previously reprimanded Kushner over his meeting with Hamas leaders, according to former Israeli consul Yaki Dayan. Dayan stated that Israel is “not completely in sync with the Americans” and that Netanyahu is not accepting the US plan for Hamas and Gaza. Israel and the US-backed Board of Peace agreed to establish two working groups: one for disarmament and demilitarization of Gaza, and another for sanitation, clean water, and public health. The Prime Minister’s Office in Jerusalem stated that disarmament must be completed promptly before any reconstruction begins. President Herzog expressed being “impressed that Israel’s security interests are an important and central element” of the proposal. Netanyahu has rejected the proposed second phase of the peace plan, insisting on Hamas's complete disarmament before Israeli withdrawal. Hamas officials insisted that an Israeli withdrawal and an end to “all forms of aggression” were a “fundamental prerequisite” for their disarmament.

title: Iranian Drones Target Iraqi Kurdistan Prime Minister's Office
summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the drone attack on the office of the Kurdistan Democratic Party leader on Monday, posting on X/Twitter that “Kurdish friends” should be aware of “false-flag ploys.” Araghchi stated that such ploys aim to “sow discord between neighbors.” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Ismaeil Baqaei doubled down on Araghchi's statements, describing the attack as “highly suspicious” and indicating Iraqi intelligence was holding groups responsible for “sinister plots.” Two Hadid-110 drones targeted the office of Masrour Barzani, the Kurdistan Regional Government's (KRG) prime minister, and the home of the region's intelligence chief in northern Iraq on Monday. title: Ebola Outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo Becomes Deadliest in History
summary: WHO Spokesperson Tarik Jašarević stated on August 18 that the Ebola virus is circulating in unknown places, with infected people outside treatment centers and undetected transmission chains. The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has become the deadliest in the country's history, with at least 2,325 deaths among 4,945 confirmed cases, according to Congolese health authorities. This surpasses the 2,299 deaths recorded in the 2018-2020 outbreak, which had 3,323 confirmed cases. The overall case fatality rate for the current outbreak stands at 47%. The outbreak was declared on May 15, marking the country's 17th recorded outbreak since 1976. It has spread across 55 health zones in six provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele, and Tshopo, with Ituri as the epicenter. The World Health Organization (WHO) stated earlier in August that reversing Ebola's spread was possible within three months, but signs indicate the situation has worsened, expanding to a sixth province. Thierno Balde, WHO incident manager, said containment is possible within three months if necessary resources are available. The WHO has raised about 60% of the US$115 million it seeks for the Ebola response. An extra 400 beds have been added in the past two weeks. The WHO Emergency Committee meets on August 18 to discuss the outbreak, which the UN agency deemed a global emergency on May 17. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a less common Ebola strain than the Zaire virus responsible for the 2018-2020 epidemic. There is currently no approved vaccine specifically targeting the Bundibugyo strain, though clinical trials are underway in Ituri. A genetic study published in Nature Medicine suggests the Bundibugyo virus emerged through a new animal-to-human transmission. Conflict, population mobility, and humanitarian pressures complicate surveillance. Community engagement is for effective testing, contact tracing, safe burials, and early treatment. Trish Newport, emergency coordinator for Doctors Without Borders, states that communities need more involvement in the response. Major obstacles include unpaid health workers striking, rebel group attacks, poor roads, and misinformation about Ebola.

title: Russian Missile Strike Kills 10, Injures 17 in Ukraine's Kharkiv Region
summary: A Russian missile attack on Tuesday killed 10 people in Pechenihy, a village in Ukraine's northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukrainian authorities said. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy stated the Russians launched a "brutal attack" on a busy intersection with a post office and stores, surrounded by residential buildings. The attack injured a further 17 people, according to Oleh Syniehubov, the governor of the surrounding region. The strike damaged 10 private buildings, a cafe, a post office, a store, and at least seven cars. Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office reported that preliminary information indicates Russia used two small Banderol cruise missiles. Zelenskiy posted photos showing a destroyed building, cars on fire, and emergency responders. Zelenskiy vowed to "definitely respond" to the Russian strike. He also called on Ukraine's "partners" to complement their responses with actions to put pressure on Russia and support Ukraine. The Kharkiv region, parts of which are occupied by Russian forces, has been heavily impacted since Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022. The United Nations reports that more civilians have been killed in the war in recent months than in any period since the invasion began. Russian officials reported that 620 drones flew towards the Moscow region overnight, with several people wounded and buildings hit. Moscow region Governor Andrey Vorobyov stated the "most serious consequences" were in the Pavlovsky Posad district, where a house burned down. Krymenergo, Crimea's largest power supplier, reported power outages in southern districts after Ukrainian drone attacks overnight. Russia warned Britain of "consequences" for supplying drones to Ukraine used to attack Russian territory. There was no immediate public comment from Russia on the attack in Pechenihy.

title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump's Final Appeal in E. Jean Carroll $5 Million Case
summary: The Supreme Court on Monday denied a request from President Donald Trump to reconsider his appeal of writer E. Jean Carroll’s $5 million lawsuit. This order follows the Supreme Court's initial decline to take up Trump's argument in June. The decision marks the end of Trump's efforts to overturn a $5 million jury award to Carroll. Carroll's representatives confirmed the $5 million payment was made in July, comprising the damages award plus post-judgment interest, totaling over $5.6 million. The Supreme Court issued a one-sentence order without explanation or noted dissents. Rehearings at the Supreme Court are rarely granted, with court rules prescribing them only for substantial "intervening circumstances." No request for a rehearing has been granted since the 1960s. A federal jury in 2023 found Trump liable for sexually abusing Carroll in a Manhattan department store dressing room in the 1990s and for defaming her in an October 2022 social media post. In that post, Trump called her allegations "a hoax and a lie" and stated, "This woman is not my type!" Trump has repeatedly denied the allegations. In a separate trial in 2024, a jury ordered Trump to pay $83.3 million in damages to Carroll for defaming her in 2019 when he denied her allegations of sexual abuse. Trump is appealing that $83.3 million judgment, with a petition currently pending before the justices, who are expected to decide later this year whether to take up the case. In his appeal for the $83.3 million case, Trump alleges his 2019 comments were "official" statements as president and therefore immune from legal action. Roberta Kaplan, Carroll’s attorney, stated that the jury’s unanimous verdict that Donald Trump sexually assaulted and then defamed E. Jean Carroll is now final and cannot be challenged in any court. A spokesman for Trump's legal team called the Carroll cases "Democrat-funded travesty of the Carroll Hoaxes." The Supreme Court has not yet made a decision on Trump's appeal of the separate $83.3 million defamation verdict.

title: Nvidia Provides $105 Billion Backstop for OpenAI's Massive Ohio Data Center
summary: Nvidia announced on Monday it is providing up to $105 billion for a giant OpenAI data center in Ohio, offering a backstop should the ChatGPT creator face financial challenges. This move follows last week's pact with Wall Street firms to pursue $500 billion in financing for Nvidia's graphics processing units. OpenAI will lease a massive data center in Ohio for 20 years, supported by Nvidia's financing commitment. The project will be built on the site of a former Cold War-era uranium enrichment plant in Pike County, Ohio. It could eventually grow to have 8 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, making it the largest single data center for artificial intelligence (AI). The data center will run "exclusively" on Nvidia chips. Nvidia will provide compute, with capacity expected to come online in phases in 2028. SB Energy, a subsidiary of SoftBank, will build and manage the data center at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus. SoftBank and SB Energy will invest more than $4 billion into local energy infrastructure and build at least 10 GW of new energy generation to power the data center. Nvidia will also invest $1.5 billion in SB Energy. OpenAI will commit $40 million to "support local priorities." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stated the project will have enough computing power for millions to use AI in new ways. OpenAI expects the project to create 35,000 temporary construction jobs over six years and 2,500 "long-term operating jobs." Nvidia's cash flow increased 18-fold over the past three years to $48.5 billion in the latest period. Nvidia's financing guarantee, its largest, marks a shift in scale for a common sector practice where AI developers depend on financial backing from suppliers. Nvidia previously considered a $250 billion backstop for a 10-gigawatt data center at the Ohio location. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Nvidia would cut that guarantee to less than $120 billion. Nvidia's shares fell 5% after those reports but are still up over 19% this year.

title: South Korea Stresses US Alliance After Trump Orders Reduced Military Exercises
summary: South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday stressed the importance of a solid alliance with the United States, as many South Koreans expressed bafflement and concern over President Donald Trump’s abrupt order to "substantially reduce" joint military exercises. Trump made the surprise announcement in a social media post just before the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises began on Monday. These exercises are largely designed to sharpen readiness against North Korean threats and have been held for 50 years. Trump cited his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea’s refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran as reasons for his decision. He stated the exercises are costly and send an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea. Trump told reporters in Washington on Monday that Kim Jong Un had responded to his diplomatic outreach, marking what would be their first engagement since Trump's first term. Trump said he was making the situation on the Korean Peninsula "much safer" by reducing the scale of the "war games." South Korean officials confirmed the exercises began as planned, and the Pentagon offered no public explanation of what would be cut. The Ulchi Freedom Shield involves about 18,000 South Korean personnel and integrates computer-assisted command-post training with field exercises. The U.S.-South Korean alliance was forged during the 1950-53 Korean War. Confidence in the U.S. has eroded among many South Koreans due to Trump’s tariff war and a 2025 immigration raid in Georgia that detained hundreds of South Korean workers. South Korea’s Hankook Ilbo newspaper stated Trump’s announcement "reveals the stark reality of a faltering Korea-U.S. Alliance, fueling public anxiety." Lee Jae Myung, a liberal, has called for a stronger, self-reliant defense posture. Trump also questioned U.S. support for NATO allies who have refused to contribute to the Iran war. The immediate military consequences of Trump's order remain unclear due to the Pentagon's lack of public explanation regarding specific cuts.

title: Tupac Shakur Murder Trial Begins 30 Years After Rapper's Death
summary: The murder trial of former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis began on Tuesday in Las Vegas, 30 years after the 1996 killing of US rapper Tupac Shakur. Davis is the first person prosecuted in the case. Davis, 63, is charged in Clark County, Nevada, with a single count of murder using a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors argue Davis planned the shooting in retaliation for the beating of his nephew, Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, by Shakur's entourage outside a boxing match at the MGM Grand hours before the shooting on September 7, 1996. Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors that Davis did not pull the trigger but "did plan the shooting." Palal presented videos of Shakur's entourage attacking Anderson. Prosecutors point to Davis' alleged confessions in his 2019 memoir, "Compton Street Legend," and interviews with law enforcement and media, where he described handing a gun to men in the backseat of a white Cadillac that fired on Shakur's black BMW. Prosecutors played audio of Davis explaining the moment Shakur was shot. Davis' lawyer, Michael Sanft, called the prosecution's narrative "fiction" and questioned why the Clark County District Attorney's office did not charge Davis years ago. Sanft argued that "no one corroborates any of this" and that Davis' accounts in interviews and his book could not be corroborated, suggesting Davis had a habit of talking "bullshit" and parts of his memoir were fictionalized to sell copies. Shakur died at 25 and remains a cultural icon. His killing heightened the image of violence in hip-hop culture and fueled the East Coast-West Coast rap feud. No one was charged until Davis was indicted in 2023. Members of Shakur's family, including his stepbrother Maurice "Mopreme" Shakur, attended the opening statements. The trial is expected to last weeks, with the jury to determine the facts and render a verdict.

title: Israeli Settler Confronts Palestinian American at Besieged West Bank Home
summary: An Israeli settler on Tuesday confronted Palestinian American Loui Ridi on his land in Qusra, West Bank, during a tense face-off filmed by Reuters. Ridi had raised a giant American flag over his home, hoping to deter militant settlers besieging the property. Ridi arrived in Qusra late on Monday from the U.S., fearing he could lose his property to Jewish settlers who have encircled three Palestinian homes in the village for over a week. Ridi, 46, grew up in Qusra before emigrating to Toledo, Ohio. The settler approached Ridi while holding what appeared to be a Torah and filming with a mobile phone. An Israeli military vehicle drove by, and soldiers later instructed Ridi to enter his home and told the settler it was a closed military area. The settler eventually retreated, stating, "I'll leave if they leave. We're all just guarding our territory." The siege has drawn U.S. condemnation. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries urged the Trump administration to compel the Israeli government to protect Palestinians from "violent, lawbreaking settlers." The United Nations, France, Spain, and the United Kingdom have also issued condemnations. On August 13, Israeli forces ordered families to evacuate, saying homes would be seized "to protect" them, and converted 16 homes in the town into military barracks. Israeli forces briefly detained one Israeli suspect during an overnight operation dismantling nearby outpost structures, but no other arrests of settlers have been reported. Ridi began constructing his house three years ago on land owned by his grandparents and farmed by his family for generations. He said his house is in an area that Israeli-Palestinian peace accords in the 1990s put under Palestinian Authority control. Violence in the West Bank has soared in recent months, with Israeli soldiers and settlers killing 87 Palestinians so far this year, according to Palestinian health officials. Palestinians have killed three Israelis. Fifteen Palestinians, including two children, remain trapped in their homes for a second week.

title: Tropical Storm Lala Causes Mudslides, Death, Power Outages in Hawaii
summary: As Tropical Storm Lala moved west away from Hawaii on Monday, residents on the Big Island dealt with destruction from heavy rain over the weekend. A mudslide swept through Waiohinu, a small community on the southern point of Hawaii's Big Island, destroying about a dozen homes. In nearby Naalehu, a 90-year-old woman was found dead after being reported missing during the storm, according to Governor Josh Green and Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda. Hawaii County Police Chief Reed Mahuna stated foul play was not suspected. The eye of then-Category 1 Hurricane Lala passed just 30 miles off the Big Island's coast over the weekend, bringing wind gusts over 80 mph and torrential rain. Some areas saw more than 3 feet of rain, with Kapalua in Maui County receiving 48 inches. As of Monday night local time, about 71,000 customers were still without power across the Hawaiian Islands, according to PowerOutage.com. Bridges on the Big Island were washed away, and several communities were entirely cut off. Waiohinu residents relied on each other as emergency services could not reach them. One resident reported a family with a young child barely escaped their home before it was washed away. The Hawaiian Electric utility reported "extensive damage" to the Big Island's power transmission system. All state and Hawaii County offices, public schools on Hawaii Island, and courts and judiciary facilities will remain closed Tuesday. Cleanup efforts began with crews repairing bridges and clearing fallen trees. Governor Green, who flew over and walked through the south part of the island, noted the flooding, mud, and rock poured through Naalehu, Pahala, and Waiohinu. While a hurricane has not made direct landfall in Hawaii since Iniki in 1992, Lala's closest approach as a Category 1 hurricane was 30 miles southwest of South Point on the Big Island. Lala weakened from a hurricane to a tropical storm on Sunday after lashing the state without making landfall. The storm is projected to become a hurricane again at sea and far from land by Wednesday. Additional details about the 90-year-old woman's death were not immediately available.

title: London Vigil Honors Former Cambridge Professor Jason Arday
summary: Former Cambridge professor Jason Arday died at the age of 41 on Friday, August 14, in Battersea, London. British police stated his death was "unexpected" but not "suspicious." Thousands of Britons gathered in Trafalgar Square, London, on Monday, August 17, for a vigil to mourn his passing. Organizers asked attendees to wear black and bring flowers, with around 2,000 people showing up, including Labour MP Diane Abbott and filmmaker Misan Harriman. Harriman stated the "legacy media crossed every line in the treatment of Jason," while Abbott said the campaign was led by "people who didn’t believe a black man should be a Cambridge professor." Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023, resigned on August 5 from his post as professor of sociology of education after multiple plagiarism accusations. In a public resignation letter, he stated he had "reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure." His family denounced "a campaign of sustained abuse" since his 2023 appointment and asked the press to stop the "campaign of harassment." An online fundraising page created by racial equality campaigner Patrick Vernon to support Arday's family had raised over £163,000 ($218,000) by Monday afternoon. A petition demanding a public inquiry into the media coverage had gathered over 83,000 signatures. Chris Smith, the University of Cambridge's chancellor, condemned a "racist feeding frenzy" prompted by the plagiarism claims, stating it was right to "refuse to join in." Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a Cambridge alumnus, called Arday's death "a tragedy on so many levels." Press regulator IPSO is reviewing a "high volume of complaints and concerns" over newspaper coverage, with Newscord reporting over 199,000 emails sent to IPSO. The allegations of plagiarism were first made by Nathan Cofnas, a self-described "race realist" and American philosopher who questioned Arday's background and achievements. Cofnas, who was an academic at Cambridge, is critical of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives and believes intelligence varies by ethnic background. Arday had disputed the allegations against him. He was diagnosed with autism and other developmental difficulties as a child.
