title: Mother Testifies on Lindsay Clancy's Declining Mental State
summary: The defense in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy continued calling witnesses on Tuesday, August 18, 2026, in Plymouth Superior Court. Clancy, a Duxbury woman, is charged in the deaths of her three children in January 2023. The prosecution rested its case on Monday, and the defense began by calling Clancy's sister and mother, Paula Musgrove, to the stand. Musgrove testified that in the months leading up to the children's deaths, several of her daughter’s statements and actions unsettled her, including Clancy asking to sleep in her mother’s bed. Musgrove also testified that Clancy told her the medication was "destroying" her mind and that she was having thoughts of harming her children. In December 2022, a few weeks before the killings, Clancy told Musgrove and her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, that she had "thoughts of harming the children." Musgrove recalled a desperate text from Clancy in October 2022, stating, "Mom will you please come up and stay with me for a bit? I'm really sick. Something is wrong. I had horrible insomnia all night and I just don't know how I am going to get through the day. I started taking the medicine my doctor prescribed for anxiety and I think it's made things worse. It's just really scary, and I don't want to be alone." An emergency room doctor testified as an expert witness about the injuries Clancy sustained when she cut herself and jumped from a second-story window in a failed attempt to end her life after killing her children. Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the deaths of her 5-year-old daughter Cora, 3-year-old son Dawson, and 8-month-old son Callan. She is paralyzed from the waist down and held without bail at Tewksbury State Hospital, where she receives treatment. Clancy admits to killing her children. Prosecutors, led by Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham, contend she acted intentionally and should be held criminally responsible, alleging she planned the murders before faking a suicide attempt. Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington argues she suffered from postpartum psychosis and bipolar disorder and was overmedicated, affecting her sense of reality.

title: Federal Judge Blocks Trump Administration's FBI Headquarters Move
summary: A US judge on Monday, August 17, 2026, blocked plans to move the FBI's headquarters to a federal office building in Washington, finding that President Donald Trump's administration illegally tossed out a previously approved plan. US District Judge Theodore D. Chuang, an appointee of President Barack Obama, ruled that the move was "not in accordance with law" and blocked the Trump administration from moving the FBI to the Reagan building, renovating it, or repurposing funds. The ruling is the latest development in a yearslong battle over where to house the main office for the nation's premier law enforcement agency. A site in Greenbelt, Maryland, was picked during former President Joe Biden's administration in 2023. However, Trump appointees sought to reverse that decision last year in favor of repurposing the Ronald Reagan Building, a federal office complex a few blocks from the FBI's existing headquarters. The suit was brought by the state of Maryland and Prince George's County. Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown, a Democrat, stated that Maryland and Prince George's County committed more than a decade of work to earn the FBI headquarters and pledged hundreds of millions of dollars. Brown said the ruling cleared the way for the headquarters project to return to Greenbelt. The FBI has been headquartered in downtown Washington at the J. Edgar Hoover Building since 1975, but structural problems have plagued it for the last 20 years. In July 2025, FBI Director Kash Patel announced the bureau would relocate to the Reagan Building, stating it offered "the most cost-effective and resource-efficient way to carry out our mission." Last November, Maryland sued Patel and the bureau, alleging the Trump administration attempted to "unlawfully sabotage" the 2023 plan and illegally divert over $323 million in designated congressional funding. Judge Chuang sided with Maryland, writing in a 47-page opinion that the Trump administration's move to divert funding and cancel the plan was "arbitrary and capricious and not in accordance with law," in addition to other violations of federal law.

title: FIFA COO Kevin Lamour Exits After Criticizing Gianni Infantino
summary: FIFA announced that Chief Operating Officer Kevin Lamour has left the organization, weeks after he publicly criticized Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup and other tournaments. A FIFA spokesperson confirmed on Monday, August 17, 2026, that "the working relationship between FIFA and Kevin Lamour as FIFA’s Chief Operating Officer has ended." FIFA thanked Kevin for his two years of service and wished him luck for the future, stating no further comment would be made. Lamour joined FIFA's senior leadership group in November 2024, having previously been part of the inner circle that campaigned for Infantino’s election as FIFA president in 2016. His responsibilities included overseeing finance, legal and compliance, communications, member associations, technology and operations, and social responsibility across FIFA's offices in Zurich, Paris, and Miami. Lamour had publicly criticized the proposal last month, stating FIFA staff had been "deceived" over the plan and describing it as "the project of one person." He said, "Our mission. Is to serve football, not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies FIFA when he is supposed to be at its service." Lamour's comments came soon after Carlos Cordeiro, a senior adviser to Infantino, resigned in protest against the proposal, calling it "a bad deal for football." Infantino subsequently withdrew the proposal later the same day. The proposal aimed to create a $20 billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), and sell up to a 20% stake to private equity investors to raise $4.2 billion. The plan faced widespread opposition, with three regional football governing bodies (UEFA, CONCACAF, and AFC) calling it a "fundamental breach" and stating it should not go ahead. The Oceania Football Confederation (OFC) also supported the withdrawal of the FFE proposal, emphasizing good governance, transparency, and respect for institutional processes. Human rights organization FairSquare has urged FIFA to rule Gianni Infantino ineligible to seek another term as president, arguing he has already reached the three-term limit set out in the governing body's statutes.

title: Rumor Triggers Deadly Stampede at Bihar's Ashok Dham Temple
summary: A stampede at the Ashokdham Temple in Lakhisarai district, Bihar, India, killed at least seven people and injured more than a dozen others on Monday, August 17, 2026. The incident occurred as thousands of Hindus gathered to offer prayers and perform Jal Abhishek to Lord Shiva on the third Monday of the auspicious Shravan or Sawan month. Preliminary accounts indicate at least 50,000 devotees had gathered at the site when a rumor triggered panic among the crowd. All the victims are reportedly women, and several injured individuals are in critical condition. Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced an ex-gratia of Rs 2 lakh from PMNRF (Prime Minister’s National Relief Fund) for the next of kin of each deceased and Rs 50,000 for every wounded individual. The tragedy was the result of a rumor that a live electric wire had fallen on people after a pole collapsed, but it was actually a cable wire. Officials stated that broken barricades and a swelling crowd also contributed to the stampede-like situation. The incident occurred between 6:30 and 6:45 am. Lakhisarai DM Shailendra Kumar noted the crowd swelled in an "unprecedented manner." This is the second stampede at an Indian temple this year; earlier, nine people were killed in a stampede at another temple in Bihar's Nalanda district on March 31, 2026. Rumors and panic have repeatedly turned massive gatherings across India into deadly stampedes, with past incidents including Patna’s Gandhi Maidan and temple gatherings in Ujjain. The incident highlights how misinformation, overcrowding, and poor crowd management can have devastating consequences. In Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, 13 devotees fainted at the Nagchandreshwar Temple on the same day due to overcrowding, as the temple, which opens only once a year on Nag Panchami, witnessed a rush of devotees. A stampede-like situation also erupted at the Nagchandreshwar Mandir in Ujjain, leaving at least three people injured. Rescue and medical operations were started by the administration and authorities, and the toll is feared to rise.

title: Hundreds of Migrants Protest in Ceuta as Morocco Increases Border Arrests
summary: Moroccan security forces prevented nearly 300 "irregular migrants" from crossing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Saturday and arrested hundreds of other would-be migrants in Fnideq, northern Morocco. title: Spacecraft Capture August 12 Solar Eclipse; Future Eclipses Announced
summary: Spacecraft captured views of the August 12 total solar eclipse, which plunged millions across Greenland, Iceland, and Spain into a false twilight. ESA's MTG-I1 satellite provided a view of the moon's shadow darkening Earth's surface. NASA astronaut Jessica Meir photographed a partial eclipse with approximately 18% sun coverage from the Russian segment of the International Space Station on August 12. The eclipse occurred as the moon passed directly between the sun and Earth during its new moon phase. Looking ahead, two more solar eclipses are scheduled for Spain in 2027 and 2028. A total solar eclipse will take place on August 2, 2027, around 10:50 a.m., offering easier viewing due to the sun's high position. title: Kushner Meets Netanyahu After Hamas Talks to Revive Gaza Peace Plan
summary: United States President Donald Trump's envoy Jared Kushner met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday, August 17, in Jerusalem. This meeting followed Kushner's talks with Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya in the Egyptian city of El-Alamein on Sunday, August 16. Former British prime minister Tony Blair and Nickolay Mladenov, director of the U.S.-established Board of Peace, also participated in the meeting with Netanyahu. The diplomatic efforts aim to advance Trump's Gaza peace plan, which includes a 15-point roadmap for peace in Gaza and a 20-point overall plan. Kushner's Sunday meeting with al-Hayya lasted over two hours and included mediating officials from Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey. Hamas endorsed the latest stage of Trump's Gaza plan, but Netanyahu publicly rejected the roadmap earlier this month. Netanyahu insists Hamas must be "genuinely disarmed" of all weapons before any Israeli withdrawal. Hamas states it will not disarm until Israel fulfills its ceasefire obligations and withdraws to the "yellow line." Israeli forces currently control about 60% of the Gaza Strip. Kushner demanded Hamas verify it is giving up its weapons and renounce any future role in governing Gaza. Hamas reaffirmed its commitment to demilitarize Gaza during the meeting, according to a source with direct knowledge, but a subsequent Hamas statement did not explicitly mention disarmament. Hamas is demanding the US administration compel Israel to approve the roadmap. Kushner told al-Hayya there was no room for negotiation on disarmament, warning that "the bar is high" because Israel does not trust Hamas. The Board of Peace also seeks to accelerate humanitarian aid and reconstruction in Gaza.

title: Israeli Minister Ben-Gvir Advocates Killing 30-40 Gazans Every Night
summary: Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir stated Israel should kill "30 to 40" Gazans in strikes every night. title: Trump Vows Strait of Hormuz US Territory; Iran Rejects Claim, UAE Reports Attacks
summary: Iran rejected President Donald Trump's claim on Saturday that he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a territory of the United States. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi stated on X that the strategic waterway "has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian," adding it "will only be closed and opened under Iran's command." The United Arab Emirates' state-owned oil giant ADNOC reported on Saturday that one of its vessels came under attack the night before. Abu Dhabi's Foreign Ministry blamed Tehran, asserting Iran's Revolutionary Guards were engaged in "acts of piracy" in the strait. This marks the third attack on a UAE state-owned oil vessel this week, following drone strikes on two ADNOC ships on Thursday. President Trump said on Friday he would designate the Strait of Hormuz a US territory "pretty soon" after the US defeats Iran. He delivered these remarks at a police academy in New York, also suggesting the strait is already US territory due to the naval blockade. An unnamed White House official later clarified that Trump was joking. The Strait of Hormuz is a global chokepoint through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes. Iran has blocked the passage, using it as a global economy "kill switch," while Washington has maintained a military naval blockade against Iran's ports since the war began on February 28. The memorandum of understanding signed between the two countries in June expires on Sunday. Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a top Iranian official, previously outlined conditions for reopening the strait, including an end to the "war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Iraq," an end to sanctions, release of frozen assets, and compensation for wartime damage. The April cease-fire between the United States and Iran collapsed due to attacks in the strait. US Central Command reported American forces have redirected 62 commercial vessels, disabled three, and boarded two since resuming its blockade on July 14. title: Indonesia Earthquake Death Toll Rises To 68 As New Quake Hits Flores
summary: A magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck Indonesia’s Flores region early on August 17, Monday, at a depth of around 10 kilometers. This tremor follows a powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake that hit eastern Indonesia days earlier. The death toll from the 7.7-magnitude earthquake has risen to at least 68 people, with more than 200 others injured. The National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) reported 213 injured people and 1,300 homes damaged across East Nusa Tenggara province, with nearly 250 destroyed on Flores alone. Some 5,000 people were forced into temporary shelters. Thousands of people on Flores island in East Nusa Tenggara province are waiting for aid, with many communities cut off by the quake. Landslides and damaged roads have blocked access to villages. The province's governor declared a 14-day state of emergency on Sunday. The 7.7-magnitude quake occurred shortly before 6 a.m. Saturday at a depth of 10 kilometers, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Tsunami warnings were issued but later lifted. Authorities have recorded 1,576 aftershocks into Monday, though only a small proportion were felt. Rescue teams are providing medical assistance to hundreds of injured people and digging through debris looking for anyone buried beneath landslides. They focused on three regencies that remained inaccessible: Manggarai, East Manggarai, and Nagekeo. More than 900 homes were destroyed and 450 more damaged in East Nusa Tenggara province, forcing about 5,000 people into temporary shelters. The quake affected 6,000 people who were displaced in the Sikka, Manggara, Nagekeo, Bima, and Selayar areas. Additionally, 914 homes, 93 educational facilities, 36 health facilities, and 38 government offices were damaged by the 7.7 quake.

title: Morocco Detains Hundreds of Migrants Near Ceuta Amid Mass Crossing Calls
summary: Moroccan authorities detained at least 355 people near Ceuta on Saturday, August 15, as security forces acted to prevent a mass crossing into the Spanish enclave. The mass crossing had been called for on social media. Reuters earlier reported at least 111 detentions in and around Fnideq, citing a Moroccan Interior Ministry source who identified 109 Sub-Saharan African migrants and two Moroccan citizens. Police reportedly fired tear gas at groups gathering on hills near the border. Spain deployed soldiers and hundreds of additional police officers to Ceuta. This security operation followed online calls for a mass crossing on August 15. It came two weeks after more than 72,000 people crossed into Ceuta on July 30, overwhelming the enclave. An estimated 7,000 to 9,000 migrants from the July influx remain in Ceuta, straining reception centers, hospitals, and law enforcement. Hundreds of Moroccan migrants protested in Ceuta on Sunday, demanding asylum and urging Spanish authorities not to return them to Morocco. Protesters waved Spanish flags and banners, chanting "We need asylum!" Ceuta Mayor-President Juan Jesus Vivas called for asylum claims linked to the surge to be rejected and migrants returned. Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska supported this approach, stating irregular arrivals would not be allowed to remain in Ceuta, reach mainland Spain, or obtain legal status, except in rare cases. Judicial associations insist claims must be assessed individually, arguing illegal entry does not forfeit the right to seek asylum. The crisis has revived a sovereignty dispute between Madrid and Rabat. Morocco has claimed Ceuta and Melilla since gaining independence in 1956. Spain regards the enclaves, controlled for centuries, as integral parts of its territory. Moroccan Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi said on August 11 that Rabat repeatedly raised the territories' status with Madrid and wanted the dispute resolved through negotiations. Spanish Defense Minister Margarita Robles rejected the claim, declaring Ceuta and Melilla were Spanish and "cannot be touched." Spain's Foreign Ministry said the country's territorial integrity was not open to discussion.

summary: Light rain on Monday morning aided firefighters battling Belgium's largest wildfire on record, which has burned over 3,000 hectares of the High Fens nature reserve in eastern Belgium. Many of those caught in the crush were women, with at least four of those killed identified as women aged between 44 and 55. Bihar's Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary described the deaths as "heart-wrenching" and announced compensation of 400,000 rupees ($4,180) for the family of each person killed. State minister Vijay Kumar Sinha said the circumstances surrounding the disaster would be investigated. Prime Minister Narendra Modi also expressed his condolences to the victims' families. This incident marks the second stampede at an Indian temple this year, highlighting that crowd crushes are relatively common during religious festivals in India.

title: Colombian President Asks Trump to Suspend Tariffs After Deadly Quake
summary: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella asked US President Donald Trump to temporarily suspend tariffs on Colombian products. This request aims to aid Colombia's recovery from a 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck on Monday morning, August 10. The earthquake devastated cities and towns across western Colombia, including Cali, Pereira, and Buenaventura. Official estimates on Sunday, August 16, put the death toll at around 290, with more than 140 people still missing and 4,200 injured. Nearly 27,000 homes were destroyed, and the government estimates reconstruction costs at $3.2 billion. More than two-thirds of the deaths were concentrated in Cali and Pereira. Rescue efforts continue, but hopes of finding survivors are dwindling nearly a week after the disaster. Emergency workers in Cali continued searching unstable rubble on Sunday, with Captain Alberto Hernandez of the Cali fire department stating there were "no signs of life." Aftershocks add danger for rescue crews and residents. Israel's "Alliance of Brothers" delegation, including IDF Home Front Command engineers, is assisting with search and rescue and assessing damaged buildings in western Colombia. Colombian billionaire banker Jaime Gilinski pledged 150 billion pesos ($47.75 million) to rebuild hospitals and schools in Cali, while the Santo Domingo family pledged $32 million on Friday. President de la Espriella took office earlier this month, just days before the quake, and was endorsed by Trump in the June 21 presidential runoff. He posted on X on Saturday evening, August 15, thanking Trump for emergency assistance and making the tariff request. The Trump administration has not yet responded to de la Espriella's request. The US State Department confirmed the United States pledged $26.5 million in emergency support, including health items, shelters, and food. President Trump's tariffs, covering nearly all US imports, are designed to be permanent and are based on existing US trade law. A trade economist believes consumers will bear the burden of these tariffs, which are unpopular. Trump has claimed foreigners pay for the tariffs, but US tariff invoices are sent to US businesses that import products.

title: Iran, Oman Reach 'In Principle' Deal on Hormuz Transit Route
summary: Iran announced on Monday, August 17, it reached an "in principle" understanding with Oman on a plan for ships to transit the Strait of Hormuz. The two sides are working to finalize details and issue a joint statement. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei stated "an understanding has been reached regarding the map of the transit route." The agreement is being prepared as a package, including the route map. Details suggest ships could enter the strait along a route close to Iran and exit near Oman, without paying fees or tolls during an interim period. Baghaei acknowledged negotiations moved slowly but confirmed plans to finalize the arrangement. This announcement came as a 60-day negotiating period for a broader peace deal between the United States and Iran expired without an agreement. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz slowed over the weekend, with no transits recorded on Sunday, August 16, according to Kpler tracking data. Only five cargo ships passed through the strait on Saturday, compared to 31 vessels the previous weekend. Shipping traffic hit a three-month low last week, with a five-day average of 13 vessel transits on Tuesday, August 11. Overall shipping is down 90% since the war started on February 28, when the Strait of Hormuz averaged about 130 vessel transits per day. The strait typically carries about one-fifth of the world's traded oil supplies. Iran effectively closed the strait after Israel and the US attacked the country on February 28. Reopening the waterway has been a primary focus of indirect negotiations between Iran and the US. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Iran had not decided to resume talks with the United States. Araqchi previously stated that Washington must meet Iran's conditions regarding the strait for shipping to resume.

title: Trump Orders Pentagon to Scale Back US-South Korea Military Drills
summary: President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to "substantially reduce" joint military drills with South Korea just hours before the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises were set to begin on Monday. Trump stated on Truth Social that he was "not happy" with US participation, citing the drills as "costly" and sending an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea. Trump also noted that South Korea declined his recent request to join US efforts in the denuclearization of Iran. Despite Trump's directive to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, the joint military drills between South Korea and US troops went ahead as planned on Monday. South Korea's presidential Blue House announced it is reviewing Trump's comments and expressed hope that his personal relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un could lead to meaningful talks with Pyongyang. The Blue House also stated it would continue diplomatic consultations on US-Korea military cooperation related to the Strait of Hormuz. South Korea's defense ministry confirmed it was proceeding with the annual exercise as "previously notified and scheduled." The Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises are one of two major annual drills between the allies, expected to involve approximately 18,000 South Korean troops, US forces, and personnel from 12 of the 18 member states of the United Nations Command. North Korea's Foreign Ministry had previously threatened unspecified action against the US and South Korea, describing their joint military drills as "a rehearsal for an aggressive war." summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche stated on Sunday, August 16, that he would not pledge the Justice Department would always act independently of the White House. summary: Police are looking for additional people who fired guns in the Virginia State University shooting that wounded five individuals. title: Trump's 2024 Grocery Photo Op Haunts Republicans Ahead of Midterms
summary: President Donald Trump's 2024 grocery photo op now presents a vulnerability for Republicans ahead of November's midterm elections. Two years ago, on August 15, 2024, Trump staged a press conference at his Bedminster golf club, flanked by grocery staples, to highlight inflation under Democrats. He blamed the Biden administration for sharp increases in groceries and pledged to bring down costs. A Reuters analysis of 26 grocery categories tracked by the Bureau of Labor Statistics found prices have risen 3.4 percent in the first 19 months of his second term. Sheila Carney, a 68-year-old Trump voter, expressed frustration over current grocery prices, stating, "He hasn't brought anything down." Higher petrol and grocery prices are squeezing household budgets, making the cost of living the top issue for American voters. A recent poll conducted by Focaldata for the Financial Times found 53 percent of registered voters felt worse off financially today than on January 19, 2025, when Joe Biden concluded his presidency. This includes 57 percent of independents and nearly a quarter of self-identified Republicans. Voters now give Democrats a slight edge over Republicans on who they view as better stewards of the economy, a first in nearly a decade, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Democrats also had an edge on handling jobs and the economy. Sixty-four percent of voters felt the economy was going in the wrong direction. The poll, conducted among 1,913 registered voters between August 7 and August 10, found 55 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump's job performance. His approval rating among Republicans dropped eight points between this latest poll and the Financial Times' previous survey in July. Republicans are poised to bear the brunt in November, as incumbents are more likely to be punished when gas is expensive. Fuel costs have surged since Trump launched a war on Iran, and the national average has stayed above $4 a gallon, roughly 30 percent higher than a year ago. Trump has "shrugged off" the surge in gas prices and told reporters he did not think about them. He also stated earlier this year that he "loved" inflation.

title: Trump Envoy Kushner Meets Netanyahu After Hamas Peace Talks
summary: US President Donald Trump's Middle East envoy, Jared Kushner, met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem on Monday, August 17. Trump had said the agreement would be carried out in phases, with Israeli forces withdrawing as disarmament proceeded and an "International Stabilization Force" working with a new Palestinian police force. Eight Muslim countries issued a statement on Sunday condemning Israel's rejection of the plan. Kushner was joined in the meetings by Nickolay Mladenov, Trump's Board of Peace envoy for Gaza, and former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair. Representatives of Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey, who have mediated peace efforts, were also part of the meeting in Egypt. title: DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Becomes Deadliest in Country's History
summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has become the deadliest in the country's history, with 2,325 deaths. This surpasses the previous record toll of 2,299 from an outbreak in 2018-2020. Government figures released on Monday, August 17, show 4,945 confirmed cases of the disease, including 101 detected in the previous 24 hours. The outbreak, the DRC's 17th, was declared on May 15 but health authorities now say sequencing showed it began in February. It has spread to 53 health zones across Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uele, Tshopo, and five other provinces. More than 3,400 cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported. The United Nations warned on August 14 that "Ebola is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo" and that the epidemic is killing one person every 30 minutes. The UN announced an additional $30 million in emergency funding on Friday, August 14, to help tackle the outbreak. The outbreak is now the second-largest globally in lethality, surpassed only by the West Africa outbreak in 2014-2016, which recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths. The current outbreak reached 2,000 deaths in less than three months, compared to nearly five months for the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak to reach 1,000 deaths. The case fatality ratio, the proportion of deaths following a confirmed infection, has risen from about 20% in early June to 46%. Experts say this rise reflects deficiencies in surveillance, detection, and access to care, not increased lethality of the virus. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments. Clinical trials of two possible treatments for this strain began last month in Ituri. Health agencies are battling to win the trust of local communities, which is "absolutely key to an effective Ebola response," according to Bruno Michon, Operations Manager for the IFRC's DRC Ebola response. The International Council of Nurses (ICN) wrote to DRC health minister Roger Kamba, demanding immediate action to pay and protect nurses and health workers.

title: Trump Family Crypto Firm Gets Preliminary Bank Charter Approval
summary: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) granted preliminary conditional approval on Friday for a national trust bank charter to World Liberty Trust Co., a cryptocurrency venture partially owned by President Donald Trump's family. title: Abdul El-Sayed Accused of Using Tax 'Loophole' Despite Public Stance
summary: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed faces accusations of taking advantage of a tax "loophole" despite advocating for the wealthy to "pay their fair share." Accountants told the Washington Free Beacon that El-Sayed's financial disclosure and tax return suggest he uses a compensation structure to lower his tax burden. His AME Higher LLC, an entity for consulting and speaking fees, paid him a $64,000 "salary" and $103,000 as a "member draw." This structure, commonly used to limit Social Security and Medicare tax burdens, allows S-corporation owners to pay payroll taxes only on a "reasonable salary," not on remaining profits. Robert Willens, a tax and accounting adviser, stated the split between compensation and distribution "may have been done with an eye towards tax havens." El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, a writer and assistant professor at the University of Chicago, also draws renewed scrutiny. She was arrested last fall on a felony charge for allegedly spitting on an Illinois state trooper during a protest outside an ICE facility in Chicago. Sophie Pollock, a spokesperson for the El-Sayed campaign, stated that Abdul loves his sister but "disagrees with her on a number of political positions and the rhetoric she’s chosen to use." El-Sayed's connection to Twitch streamer Hasan Piker is also a drag on him in the general election, according to one report. Representative Haley Stevens, El-Sayed's former Michigan Senate race opponent, said it "certainly makes sense" for El-Sayed to end his affiliation with Piker. Former President Barack Obama will likely campaign for El-Sayed, who won the Michigan U.S. Senate primary despite performing poorly among black primary voters. Obama previously noted that enthusiasm for Kamala Harris was weaker among "the brothers" during the 2024 presidential campaign. El-Sayed supports Medicare for All, a position Obama has also expressed support for if starting a system from scratch. The RealClearPolitics polling average shows Republican Mike Rogers up by one point against El-Sayed. A Fox poll has Rogers up by four points. El-Sayed recently attacked Rogers for "frolicking" at the Sanilac County Fair, claiming Rogers ignored servicemen and women on the USS Abraham Lincoln.

title: ISI-Backed Shahzad Bhatti Terror Network Busted, Over 200 Arrested
summary: Security agencies launched a major multi-state crackdown against the alleged ISI-backed Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN) ahead of Independence Day. Union Home Minister Amit Shah announced that over 200 operatives of the network were arrested across 14 states. Shah stated that the Modi government destroyed the SBN and thwarted its plans for subversive attacks. He described the operation as a "brilliant example of India’s zero-tolerance towards terrorism." Coordinated operations were carried out across different locations in 14 states. Substantial recoveries were made from the ISI-funded group, including improvised explosive devices (IEDs), grenades bearing Pakistan Ordnance Factory markings, pistols, live cartridges, and CCTV cameras used for espionage. The SBN is described as a Pakistan-based terror syndicate linked to grenade, IED, and petrol bomb attacks, targeted killings, and espionage activities across India. The network also paid local conduits to recce police, defense, and religious sites, and to install CCTV cameras for espionage. The National Investigation Agency (NIA) is probing multiple cases against Bhatti. These include an alleged link to the March 2025 grenade attack at the residence of social media influencer Roger Sandhu in Jalandhar, Punjab. In April 2026, the NIA chargesheeted Bhatti as an absconder, along with one other accused in that case. The anti-terror agency also found that Bhatti masterminded the November 2025 explosion at the Women Police Station, Sirsa, Haryana, and the January 2026 blast at Baldev Nagar police station in Ambala, Haryana. title: Hurricane Lala Damages Homes, Cuts Power to Thousands in Hawaii
summary: Hurricane Lala left a trail of destruction across Hawaii over the weekend, damaging homes, destroying transportation links, and leaving hundreds of thousands of residents without electricity. Dramatic videos show floodwaters washing over roads, tearing through infrastructure, and cutting off communities after days of torrential rain and hurricane-force winds. The storm weakened to a tropical storm on Sunday as it moved west away from the islands. The heaviest rainfall from Lala was recorded at Laupāhoehoe on Hawaii Island's northern coast, where 42.69 inches fell between Friday and Sunday. More than 31 inches of that total came within 24 hours. Nahuku recorded over 35 inches of rainfall, while Hilo International Airport received nearly 10 inches. This deluge contributed to severe flooding, mudslides, and fast-moving torrents that overwhelmed roads and streams in parts of Hawaii Island. Governor Josh Green stated at least 100 homes were damaged or destroyed during the storm. State officials reported infrastructure damage across multiple islands. The Hawaii Department of Transportation released videos showing floodwaters overtaking roadways, and emergency officials reported extensive washouts in hard-hit areas. Local reporting from Maui Now indicated several occupied homes were "inundated" by floodwaters on Hawaii Island, prompting search-and-rescue operations involving local agencies, the National Guard, and the Coast Guard. Power outages remained a consequence, with more than 180,000 households without power across Hawaii on Sunday afternoon. This number had dropped from over 220,000 to about 130,000 by Sunday morning. Outages were particularly noted in Oahu, the most populated island. Hawaiian Electric warned on Saturday evening that repair efforts were hampered by hurricane-force winds and flooded roadways. State officials urged residents to stay indoors after at least one person was reported dead in a car-related accident. Two homes were swept away, according to the National Weather Service. About 117 people were in shelters as of Sunday morning.

title: Four Antonello da Messina Artworks Stolen from Messina Museum
summary: Four works by Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen from the regional museum in Messina, Sicily, during an annual religious festival on Saturday. The theft occurred on the Feast of the Assumption, while hundreds of devotees and onlookers were paying homage to the Vara procession in Piazza Duomo, 4 km away from the museum. Three or four people, with faces covered by balaclavas, managed to enter the museum shortly before 10:00 PM. They stole six works by Antonello, the most important Sicilian painter of the 15th century. Two other works were found shortly afterward on a low wall outside the museum, likely abandoned by the thieves during their escape due to passersby. The heist is estimated to be worth tens of millions of euros. Art expert Alberto Fiz estimated the value of the stolen works at 70 million euros ($81 million) to 80 million euros ($92 million). The stolen pieces included three of the five surviving panels from Antonello's 1473 "San Gregorio Polyptych" and a small, double-sided tempera panel dating back to 1465-1474. The double-sided panel features the Virgin and Child with a Franciscan Monk on its front and Christ in Pietà on its reverse. The perpetrators cut through metal perimeter fencing and forced open a side door to enter the gallery halls. They then breached an armored glass display case to extract the double-sided panel. Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli expressed "dismay and regret," assuring "his full willingness to cooperate with the regional authorities." Sicilian Regional President Renato Schifani described it as an "exceptional criminal act" and an "intolerable affront to universal cultural heritage." The Messina Public Prosecutor's Office opened an investigation into aggravated theft of artworks, currently against unknown persons, as Chief Prosecutor Antonio D'Amato emphasized. Police set up checkpoints at ferry terminals to Calabria, but checks have been unsuccessful. It remains unknown whether the gang left Sicily or if the masterpieces are hidden on the island.

title: African Union Reopens Khartoum Office Amid Sudan Conflict
summary: The African Union has reopened its liaison office in Khartoum, signaling a commitment to resolving the war in Sudan that has lasted over three years. The AU's decision to re-establish a physical presence in the capital aims to provide on-the-ground technical support and maintain open communication channels with Sudan's warring parties. AU personnel had withdrawn in April 2023 when fighting erupted, forcing the organization to conduct virtual diplomacy from its headquarters in Addis Ababa. The AU has a history of mediating conflicts in Sudan, including its role in advancing the 2005 peace agreement and facilitating the August 2019 power-sharing agreement after the coup that toppled Omar al-Bashir. The office was previously led by Mohamed Belaiche, the AU Commission Chairperson’s Special Representative to Sudan. Sudan's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Mohi-Eddin Salem, described the visit by AU ambassadors and members of the African Peace and Security Council to Khartoum as historic, stating it followed the "liberation of Khartoum, the defeat of the terrorist militia, and the restoration of security and stability to the capital." During a meeting with the delegation, a documentary film was shown detailing alleged crimes committed by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia. Algeria's Permanent Representative to the AU and Chairperson of the African Peace and Security Council, Ambassador Mohamed Khaled, affirmed the AU's solidarity with Sudan and its commitment to restoring security and stability while respecting state sovereignty.

summary: Four artworks by 15th-century painter Antonello da Messina were stolen overnight from the Museo Regionale di Messina, Italian media reported. title: President Trump Orders Navy to Restore Steam Catapults on Ford-Class Carriers
summary: President Donald Trump signed a national security memorandum on Thursday ordering the U.S. Navy to return to using steam catapults for launching jets from aircraft carriers. The directive also includes replacing advanced weapons elevators with hydraulic systems. The immediate target for these changes is the USS Doris Miller (CVN-81), the fourth Ford-class carrier, which is currently under construction. The memorandum orders Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, in consultation with the secretary of the Navy, to present a plan within 60 days. This plan must detail the timelines and resources required to replace the Doris Miller's Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) with traditional steam catapults and its advanced weapons elevators with hydraulic systems. The order does not require ripping electromagnetic catapults out of carriers already in service, such as the USS Gerald R. Ford, USS John F. Kennedy, and USS Enterprise, which will remain untouched. A steam catapult uses high-pressure steam to propel a jet along a track, while an electromagnetic catapult is digitally controlled and uses electric and linear motors to generate an electromagnetic field. Experts have warned that this move will cost taxpayers billions of dollars. The Navy and industry leaders have long opposed returning to steam catapults due to the costs involved. Installing electromagnetic catapults and elevators was an integral aspect of the Ford-class design and contributed to the class's slow delivery and commissioning. President Trump has expressed his preference for steam catapults for nearly a decade, dating back to a May 2017 interview with Time magazine during his first term. He described the digital system as "very complicated" and said, "You're going to goddamned steam." The topic has frequently appeared at rallies and other events. The directive comes as the U.S. military seeks funding from Congress and the Navy struggles to staff its ships.

title: Kennedy Center Board Votes to Inscribe Trump's Name, Close for Renovations
summary: The Kennedy Center board voted Thursday to add President Donald J. Trump's name to the building's facade and close the center for two years for renovations. This decision marks a second attempt to place the president's name on the building, following a May ruling by U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper. The physical site will also be renamed "President Donald J. Trump Plaza." title: Putin Visits Disputed Kuril Islands, Angering Japan
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin made his first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril Islands on Thursday, drawing strong condemnation from Japan. Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the visit "absolutely unacceptable," asserting the islands are "inherently Japanese territory" and that Tokyo had "repeatedly requested the Russian side to ensure that the president does not visit the Northern Territories." Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also protested the visit, and Japan summoned Nikolay Nozdrev, Russia's ambassador in Tokyo, to lodge a strong protest. The Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories, are a sparsely populated volcanic archipelago. The Soviet Union annexed the four southernmost islands (Etorofu/Iturup, Kunashiri, Shikotan, and the Habomai islet group) at the end of World War II. During his trip, Putin visited the island of Iturup, where Russia operates a military base, touring a fish processing complex, a hospital, and a school, and meeting with Sakhalin regional governor Valery Limarenko. Japan renounced claims to the Kuril Islands in the 1951 Treaty of San Francisco but did not recognize Soviet sovereignty. The territorial dispute has prevented a peace treaty between Tokyo and Moscow since the war. Japan is now considering taking measures against Russia, potentially including additional sanctions. The United States backs Japan's position on Putin's trip. Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev stated the Kuril Islands will "forever remain Russian land" and warned of "monstrous consequences" if Japan continues its claim. Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War suggested Putin's visit is a response to Japan's recent defense white paper, which identified Moscow as a critical threat. Japan's ties with Russia have deteriorated since the 2022 conflict in Ukraine, with Japan joining G7 sanctions.

title: Trump Signs Executive Order Overhauling Childhood Vaccine Recommendations
summary: US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday recommending a reduction in the number of diseases covered by universal routine childhood vaccination recommendations from 18 to 11. The order also advocates for splitting the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate shots, to be administered at separate visits. Separate measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines are currently not available in the US. Marco Cavaleri, head of the European Medicines Agency's Public Health Threats Department, stated that such decisions could lead to immunization gaps, leaving populations vulnerable to outbreaks and fueling mistrust in vaccines. The order moves recommendations for COVID-19, influenza, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, RSV, and hepatitis An and B away from universal routine vaccination. Some immunizations will remain recommended for children considered at higher risk, while others will be subject to "shared clinical decision-making" between parents and healthcare providers. The World Health Organization (WHO) chief, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, stated on Wednesday that the current evidence is "unequivocal: vaccines, including the MMR vaccine, are safe and do not cause autism." Kennedy Jr., has questioned vaccine safety and promoted claims linking vaccines to autism. Trump claimed, without evidence, that the current combined MMR shot could be "quite lethal." The executive order is an attempt to reinstate sweeping changes to the vaccine schedule made earlier this year by Kennedy Jr., which a federal judge later halted. However, an executive order can only offer guidance to agencies and does not change laws or set recommendations. Recommendations from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the federal agency that sets vaccine guidance, remain the same. title: Danube Low Levels Force Romania Nuclear Plant Shutdown; Spain Extends Operations
summary: Romania shut down its last working nuclear reactor on Thursday due to an and ongoing drop in the Danube River's water level. title: Putin Visits Disputed Kuril Islands, Japan Lodges Strong Protest
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the Kuril Islands on Thursday, August 13, 2026, traveling to Iturup, which Japan calls Etorofu. Moscow has bolstered its military presence on the Kurils over the years. Mr. Putin's trip followed his attendance at the final stage of exercises involving Russia's Pacific Fleet off Sakhalin Island. title: Senator Demands Answers on USS Abraham Lincoln Conditions After 250 Days
summary: Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat from Connecticut, demands answers from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth regarding living conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. The vessel has been deployed in the Middle East for over 250 days, surpassing any previous US aircraft carrier deployment without a port stop. Reports indicate food shortages, broken plumbing, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in mail services. The Military Times and Stars and Stripes reported that multiple sailors on the carrier considered suicide or attempted to jump overboard, according to their family members. CBS News reported a sailor went overboard last month and was recovered safely, with circumstances under investigation. The USS Abraham Lincoln, carrying about 5,000 people, left San Diego in November for the South China Sea before being rerouted to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February. Its deployment was originally set to end in May but has been repeatedly extended with no announced return date. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called the reports "completely misrepresented" on Thursday, stating the government ensures every ship and crew has necessary provisions. However, text messages from a sailor shared with MeidasTouch describe a lack of fresh food, including no milk for three months, and a belief that the Navy does not care. Family members have raised concerns about the conditions, with Annabelle Loma stating her husband is on medical hold after trying to jump from the carrier. Maria Rodriguez reported her husband prevented another man from jumping overboard. A U.S. Navy spokesperson stated no increase in reported suicidal ideation or attempts aboard the ship has been identified, and religious, medical, and mental health professionals are available. Senator Blumenthal has given the Navy two weeks, until August 27, to provide answers. Senator Ruben Gallego called for an official oversight visit with a bipartisan Senate Delegation to the USS Lincoln.
consensus_points: Senator Richard Blumenthal has demanded answers from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth regarding conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
The USS Abraham Lincoln has been deployed in the Middle East for over 250 days, exceeding its original deployment schedule.
Reports from family members and some outlets indicate issues such as food shortages, broken plumbing, and deteriorating mental health among sailors.
Multiple reports cite instances of sailors attempting or considering suicide, or trying to jump overboard.
The U.S. Navy states it has not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or attempts aboard the ship and provides mental health professionals.
divergence_points: International sources like Al Jazeera and The Independent, along with US sources like The Daily Beast, emphasize the human impact of the conditions, including direct quotes from sailors' text messages and family members' accounts of attempted suicides.
BBC News and CBS News mention a sailor going overboard and being recovered safely, with an investigation underway, while other outlets focus more broadly on attempted suicides.
Newsweek and The Epoch Times highlight the Navy's denial of an increase in suicidal ideation or attempts, providing the official counter-statement.
The Daily Beast and Newsweek frame the situation as a "crisis" or "nightmare" for sailors in "Trump's War," linking the conditions to the ongoing conflict with Iran.

title: Colombia Earthquake Rescue Efforts Enter Final Phase as Death Toll Rises
summary: The Mexican volunteer rescue group Topos Azteca arrived in Colombia to assist with rescue efforts following the magnitude 7.4 earthquake. Rescue operations are entering their "final phase" as the critical 72-hour window for finding survivors under rubble nears its end. The earthquake, which struck western Colombia on Monday morning, August 10, has killed 265 people, injured more than 3,500, and left nearly 500 missing, according to local authorities. Civilian-run databases, however, put the number of missing at over 4,100. More than 25,800 families have been affected, and over 11,000 dwellings have been destroyed. Emergency crews in cities like Cali and Pereira worked through a third night, using bare hands, cranes, and sniffer dogs, pausing every 30 minutes to listen for signs of life. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder stated rescue efforts were "entering the final phase," though survivors could still be found. In Pereira, rescuers detected possible signs of life from street vendor Pablo Loaiza, trapped in a collapsed bakery, prompting relatives to gather. Daniela Largo, 32, was rescued alive from rubble in Pereira late Tuesday after 36 hours, following a 12-hour complex operation. A three-month-old baby was also found alive under rubble in Cali. Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, declared the disaster an "economic emergency" and announced three days of national mourning. He initially limited requests for international assistance, insisting Colombian capacities were sufficient, but later agreed to receive brigades and equipment from countries like the United States and Argentina. The Latin American and Caribbean Episcopal Council (CELAM) expressed solidarity with Colombia, mourning the loss of life. A Chabad house in Salento was damaged, but no injuries were reported.
consensus_points: A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, August 10, killing at least 265 people.
Rescue efforts are entering their "final phase" as the critical 72-hour window for finding survivors under rubble approaches its end.

title: Iran Mocks Trump's Secret Aircraft Switch Amid Missile Threat
summary: Iran's state media and its embassy in South Africa are mocking U.S. President Donald Trump over his secret aircraft switch during a visit to Turkey last month. A presenter on state television called the episode a source of "humiliation" for Trump, stemming from fear of Iran's military power. The Iranian embassy's X account shared a meme depicting Trump inside a catering box. Tehran also rejected Trump's claim of U.S. "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz, with Hossein Taeb, head of Iran's Basij paramilitary unit, asserting Iran's management and control. The secret aircraft switch was prompted by a credible and imminent threat that Air Force One could be targeted by a shoulder-fired missile, according to a person briefed on the matter. The threat emerged on the final day of Trump's visit to Ankara for the NATO summit on July 8, amid heightened tensions due to the ongoing U.S. war on Iran. U.S. officials were alarmed to discover Iranians knew Trump's exact location in Ankara, including his hotel floor. The Secret Service deemed the threat credible, leading to an extraordinary operation to conceal the president's movements. Trump and a small group of aides used a catering truck to transfer from the larger Air Force One to a smaller, nondescript C-32A jet for the flight out of Turkey. Air Force One departed separately, carrying senior administration officials, White House staff, and the traveling press corps, who were unaware of the switch. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth were aware of the switch. Trump stated on Tuesday, August 11, that the switch was the decision of the Secret Service and the U.S. military, and he believed the plane he flew on was at "greater risk."
consensus_points: President Donald Trump secretly switched aircraft during his departure from Turkey last month due to a credible missile threat.
The Secret Service deemed a threat of a shoulder-fired missile targeting Air Force One to be credible and imminent.
Trump and a small group of aides used a catering truck to transfer from Air Force One to a smaller C-32A jet.

Independent outlets like Twitchy and Townhall emphasize the media's reaction to being used as "decoys" and criticize reporters for making the story about themselves rather than the assassination threat.
Reuters and Cyprus Mail report that Tehran has not officially commented on the allegations or the airplane switch, while other sources directly quote Iranian state media's mockery.

title: Iran Rejects Trump Claims of US Control Over Strait of Hormuz
summary: Robert Murrett, a retired U.S. Navy vice admiral, states Iran's "cheap, affordable weapons" help maintain the Strait of Hormuz threat. Iran's central military command spokesperson, Ebrahim Zolfaghari, rejected US President Donald Trump's claims of US control over the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, calling them "nothing more than lies and fabrications." Zolfaghari asserted the Strait of Hormuz remains under the complete management and control of the Islamic Republic of Iran. He added that no commercial ship or tanker can pass without permission and supervision from Iranian armed forces. On Wednesday, President Trump claimed on Truth Social that the US "has total control over the Strait of Hormuz" and stated, "I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!" He also described the US Naval Blockade as "A WALL OF STEEL." Trump had previously stated Tuesday night that the US has "total control" and "We own it." Hojjatoleslam Hossein Taeb, head of Iran's paramilitary Basij forces, also said the Strait of Hormuz is "under Iran's control and management." Iran's joint military command, Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, stated no vessel can transit without Tehran's permission. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the United States has "miscalculated" on the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has maintained control of Hormuz since the war outbreak on February 28, requiring vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees. Before the war, a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas transited the strait. The US subsequently imposed a naval blockade on Iranian shipping and ports. Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is near a three-month low, with a five-day average of around 13 vessels on Tuesday, down from over 100 vessels a day before the conflict. Bret Baier reported that traffic has slowed to a trickle, with eight vessels crossing Monday and 14 on Tuesday. The International Energy Agency reports global crude oil inventories fell by 2.2 million barrels a day in July. The Energy Information Administration raised its forecast for the average price of a gallon of gasoline by 14 cents and Brent Crude from $82 to $87 a barrel for 2026.
consensus_points: Both the United States and Iran make competing claims of control over the Strait of Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump claims the United States has "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian military and political officials assert the Strait of Hormuz is under Iran's complete management and control.
Iran states no commercial vessel or tanker can pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission and supervision.
Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has slowed, reaching near three-month lows.
divergence_points: Some US outlets, including The Daily Beast and The Wall Street Journal, highlight evidence contradicting President Trump's claims of total US control, such as slowed ship traffic.
International outlets like Channel News Asia and Al Jazeera focus on Iran's direct rejection of Trump's claims and its assertion of full control over the waterway.

title: Former US Marine Robert Gilman Returns Home After Russian Detention
summary: Former U.S. Marine veteran Robert Gilman returned home "very frail" after more than 1,660 days in Russian custody, according to Kieran Ramsey, a representative for the Gilman family, on Wednesday. Gilman was unable to walk off the plane and requires extensive mental, psychological, physical, and dental care for a lengthy recovery. Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Ed Markey stated Gilman was subjected to "physical torture, forced medication and provocations" by the Russian government.
consensus_points: Former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman was released from Russian detention on Tuesday.
His release occurred on humanitarian grounds, following a pardon approved by Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Gilman had been held in Russia since January 2022, serving a sentence for assaulting a police officer and other charges.
U.S. President Donald Trump announced Gilman's release and his return to American soil.
Gilman's health had deteriorated during his detention, with reports of him being in a "catatonic-like state" and requiring extensive medical care.

title: Flock Safety Tightens Privacy Controls Amid Police Misuse Allegations
summary: Flock Safety announced policy changes Thursday, August 13, to address the misuse of its automated license plate reader technology by law enforcement officers. The company will expand its "Audit Assistance" feature, making it mandatory for all customers by the end of the year, which tracks abnormal activity and suspends user accounts during review. Officers will now be required to input case codes connected to an investigation for searches, a feature optional since July 2025, though it can be bypassed in emergencies. Flock also shortens the standard data retention window from 30 days to seven, allowing longer preservation only for evidence tied to a case number. Additionally, agencies can now decide which types of criminal offenses they share data about with other municipalities, such as blocking searches related to immigration enforcement. These changes follow revelations of officers misusing Flock's technology. Earlier this week, a police officer in New Bedford, Massachusetts, was accused in court of using the technology to stalk an ex-girlfriend. The Institute for Justice launched a database Wednesday documenting over 100 cases of alleged abuse. Some cities, including Glocester, Narragansett, South Kingstown, New Bedford, and Grass Valley, have canceled or paused their contracts with Flock Safety amid growing privacy concerns. Flock CEO Garrett Langley stated the changes will drive accountability and are a "continuation of our commitment to both safety and privacy." Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union, dismissed the announcement as largely a public relations stunt, calling several changes "retreads of previous inadequate safety measures." Marlow praised the proposed change to shrink data retention as a potentially positive step, but noted officers have previously found ways around similar safeguards, such as using generic terms like "investigation" or mocking prompts.
consensus_points: Flock Safety announced new policy changes on Thursday, August 13, aimed at addressing privacy concerns and misuse of its automated license plate reader technology.
The changes include making an audit assistance feature mandatory for all customers and shortening the default data retention period from 30 days to seven days.
Law enforcement officers will now be required to enter case codes for searches, a feature previously optional.
These policy adjustments follow multiple reports and arrests of law enforcement officers accused of misusing Flock cameras for personal or unauthorized surveillance.
Civil liberties advocates, such as the ACLU, have expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of some of the new measures, while acknowledging the data retention change as a positive step.
divergence_points: The Record and MIT Technology Review emphasize the American Civil Liberties Union's critical perspective, highlighting Chad Marlow's dismissal of the changes as a "public relations stunt" and his concerns about officers circumventing new safeguards.

Business Insider provides specific examples of Flock camera misreads leading to innocent people being stopped at gunpoint or detained, and reports that in one California town, Flock misread license plates in 71% of alerts.

title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Black Sea Port; Russia Hits Ukrainian Danube Grain Hub
summary: Russia struck Ukraine's largest grain shipment port on the Danube overnight on August 13, causing damage and setting off a fire. This attack followed Ukraine's August 12-13 assault on Novorossiysk, a major Russian Black Sea grain hub. The Ukrainian operation hit warships at a naval base and forced two major grain terminals to halt operations. Regional Governor Veniamin Kondratyev reported at least two people, including an eight-year-old child, were killed and 24 injured in Novorossiysk. Mayor Andrei Kravchenko stated the port suspended its water supply and declared an emergency, with damage to four enterprises, over two dozen residential buildings, and educational facilities. Ukraine's SBU security service described the Novorossiysk attack as having "strategic significance." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said two frigates, a large landing ship, a corvette, and other vessels were hit, calling it a "unique" operation. Russia's agriculture ministry is working to redirect export flows to alternative routes. Russia's main grain lobby group warned last month that Ukrainian attacks could shut down Black Sea grain exports. Chicago wheat futures rose around 3% after the Novorossiysk attack. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine of seeking to "provoke chaos" on the global food market. US Vice President JD Vance requested in late July that Ukraine not target Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure and non-Russian vessels, provided they were not under Ukrainian sanctions or carrying Russian oil or cargo. Ukraine agreed to this request. US officials confirmed the request, stating CPC is a "vital conduit of Kazakhstan-origin energy for European markets." Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter, and Ukraine is also a major agricultural exporter, with around 90% of its crop exports typically moving through the Black Sea. Moldova offers a rail lifeline for Ukrainian food exports. Russia intensified its campaign against ports around Odesa in July, with 35 attacks on vessels in ports, 22 on ships at sea, and 67 on port facilities. On August 9, Russian forces struck the Mayaki bridge linking Odesa toward Moldova and Romania.
consensus_points: Ukraine launched an attack on Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk on August 12-13, damaging naval assets and grain terminals.
Russia responded with an attack on Ukraine's largest grain shipment port on the Danube on August 13.
The attacks on grain infrastructure by both sides have raised concerns about global food prices and supply disruptions.
US Vice President JD Vance requested Ukraine cease attacks on certain oil tankers and infrastructure in the Black Sea, to which Ukraine agreed.
Casualties were reported in Novorossiysk, including at least two deaths and multiple injuries.
divergence_points: Some outlets, including Global News and The Independent, provide specific details on the US request to Ukraine regarding oil tankers and CPC infrastructure, including the involvement of US Vice President JD Vance.
Al Jazeera and France 24 emphasize the immediate tit-for-tat nature of the grain port attacks and their implications for global food security.
CNBC and The Moscow Times detail the specific Russian grain terminals affected and their export capacities, while other reports offer a more general overview of damage.

title: Former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji, Economic Reformer, Dies at 97
summary: Tributes for former Premier Zhu Rongji reflect nostalgia for an era when China was opening to the world and the future seemed more prosperous and hopeful. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim described Zhu as "a good friend" in a social media tribute, noting their work to strengthen economic ties and a personal bond. Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong called Zhu an "old friend," highlighting his support for a joint economic megaproject, the US$20 billion industrial park in Suzhou, established in 1993 with Lee Kuan Yew. Former US Treasury secretary Larry Summers stated Zhu was "as formidable an economic policymaker as any I have ever encountered." Zhu Rongji, former Chinese premier, died on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, at the age of 97. Xinhua, China's official news agency, announced his death in Beijing of an unspecified illness. Zhu served as premier from 1998 to 2003. He is remembered for his role in integrating China's economy into the global system. He spearheaded China's accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001, paving the way for an export boom. This fueled China's transformation into the world's second-biggest economy. Zhu oversaw domestic market reforms, including closing hundreds of loss-making state enterprises and laying off some 30 million workers. He promoted entrepreneurship, introduced foreign management expertise, and revived Chinese enterprises. During his tenure as Shanghai's mayor from 1988 to 1991, Zhu restructured the city’s industrial base, focused on exports, and initiated the Pudong New Area development zone. He recognized foreign direct investment as key to Shanghai's future growth. As governor of the People's Bank of China in 1993, he addressed "triangular debt" by injecting funds, establishing borrower responsibility, and allowing bankruptcies. He also steered the nation through the Asian Financial Crisis. Zhu was known for his sharp intellect, no-nonsense demeanor, and candid diplomacy. Zhang Chongqing, honorary president of China Group Companies Association, described Zhu as "intelligent, insightful, outspoken and decisive." Buchung Tsering, research director at the International Campaign for Tibet, stated that Zhu's legacy for Tibetans is one of increasing Beijing's political control through economic means.
consensus_points: Former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji died on Wednesday, August 12, 2026.
Zhu Rongji played a central role in China's economic reforms and its integration into the global economy.

Zhu Rongji served as premier from 1998 to 2003.
He was known for his decisive, outspoken, and reformist approach to economic policy.
divergence_points: Some outlets, including The New York Times and South China Morning Post, report Zhu Rongji died at age 97, while others, such as Radio Free Asia and Bernama, state he was 98.
The New York Times and South China Morning Post emphasize the nostalgic reflection on Zhu Rongji's era as a time of hope and opening, contrasting it with the current rigidity.

title: Houthi Attacks Kill Six in Red Sea, Escalating Shipping Tensions
summary: Six people were killed in Houthi attacks on a commercial vessel in the Red Sea near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on Tuesday, Yemen's coastguard reported. The vessel, identified as the "Tihama," was carrying weapons according to the Houthis, while Yemen's Transport Ministry stated four crew members and two Yemeni rescue personnel were killed. Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar confirmed three Pakistani nationals were killed and one injured, condemning the attack as a violation of international law and a threat to maritime security. This marks the first fatalities in a Houthi strike on shipping since the Iran war began on February 28. The Houthis also targeted Yemeni government military sites in eastern Yemen, killing at least 30 government soldiers, and attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan oil refinery. In response, Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, stated the government would not accept "a new truce" and "no action by the Houthi militias will go unanswered." Saudi crude exports from the Red Sea are increasingly switching off tracking signals to avoid Houthi attacks, with analysts noting "dark voyages." Vessel numbers through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait have decreased to 32 from 50. The Houthis declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia on July 20, targeting the U.S. and its allies in the Iran conflict.

title: Rep. Max Miller Sued Over Nude Photo of Daughter
summary: Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, is being sued by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, for allegedly "recklessly" publishing a nude photograph of their two-year-old daughter online. The lawsuit, filed Wednesday, stems from a Dropbox folder Miller posted on X on August 2, containing documents he claimed would vindicate him from domestic abuse allegations. Moreno, who is suing Miller and his attorney Aaron Minc, alleges the nude image of their daughter, "depicting her genitalia," was among the documents. The lawsuit states Miller "recklessly and intentionally provided Minc a trove of documents and photos, indifferent about what they contained or how they were used." The image was reportedly available online for approximately 23 hours before being taken down. Moreno is seeking $150,000 in damages for each time the photo was downloaded. Miller has vehemently denied all abuse allegations, including claims that he poured hot water on Moreno, pointed a gun at her head, and broke their daughter's collarbone. Moreno is the daughter of Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller's leadership PAC, Dependable Conservative Leadership PAC, has also drawn criticism for donating to Republican candidates amid these allegations. Bob Brooks criticized Rep. Ryan Mackenzie for receiving $2,500 from Miller's PAC, and Will Lawrence criticized Rep. Tom Barrett for receiving the same amount.

The lawsuit alleges a nude photograph of their daughter was published online.
The photograph was reportedly included in a Dropbox folder shared by Miller.

title: Jellyfish, Extreme Weather Reduce French Nuclear Capacity; Romania Plant Shuts
summary: Romania's state-owned nuclear power producer Nuclearelectrica plans to shut down its last working reactor on August 13 due to falling water levels on the Danube river. The two reactors at Nuclearelectrica's Cernavoda power plant typically supply about a fifth of Romania's electricity. Romania has declared an energy emergency through August, taking measures such as dredging the channel and sinking rock-filled barges. Romanian naval forces also carried out a controlled underwater explosion on the riverbed last week to improve water flow to the plant's cooling systems. In France, the country recorded a more than 20 percent shortfall in nuclear power production capacity on Wednesday, a record deficit. This was caused by environmentally related outages linked to drought, extreme heat, and a jellyfish invasion. Between 9:45 am and 10:00 am, EDF's nuclear fleet experienced a new peak in outages due to "environmental constraints" or "external environmental causes." Thirteen of EDF's 57 reactors were affected, with eight completely shut down and five operating at reduced power. Much of the lost generating capacity resulted from full or partial shutdowns at five of the six reactors at the Gravelines nuclear power plant. A swarm of jellyfish clogged pumps used to cool the units there. EDF reported around 100kg of jellyfish arrived on Saturday, increasing to "several tens of tons" by Monday. This marks the second successive year a jellyfish swarm has shuttered reactors at Gravelines. EDF had installed cameras and deployed fishing boats to patrol the area after last year's incident. Fishing vessels now conduct "preventive fishing operations" 24 hours a day with three boats patrolling off the coast. Outside Gravelines, other reactor shutdowns or reductions are linked to extreme heat and droughts, which deprive plants of cooling water. France uses nuclear power to generate around 70 percent of its electricity. Nicolas Goldberg, an energy expert at Colombus Consulting, states this situation does not pose short-term supply problems.
consensus_points: France experienced a record deficit of over 20 percent in nuclear power production capacity on Wednesday.
This deficit was caused by environmentally related outages, including drought, extreme heat, and a jellyfish invasion.

Some sources, including Euractiv, focus solely on the impending shutdown of Romania's nuclear plant due to low Danube levels.

title: US Ambassador Calls Settler Siege of Palestinian Homes 'Horrific Act of Terror'
summary: U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee condemned the actions of Israeli settlers besieging three Palestinian homes in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra as a "horrific act of terror." The settlers have surrounded the homes for several days, including one owned by a Palestinian American, Lou Ridi, and have reportedly thrown stones, attempted to bring down a stone wall, and prevented occupants from leaving despite dwindling supplies. Israeli troops intervened, dismantling "two illegal outposts" near the homes and detaining one Israeli. The military stated troops "will not operate in the home of the Palestinian family." Qusai Abu Rida, Lou Ridi's brother, stated that settlers are still present in the surroundings and "the danger has not gone away." He recounted an incident where an ambulance carrying his injured niece was turned back by the army and settlers. The U.S. believes Israel is not doing enough to prevent settler violence, according to a senior White House official. The Israeli military chief of staff ordered an additional infantry battalion to reinforce the sector. title: Luigi Mangione Expected to Plead Guilty to Federal Stalking Charges
summary: Luigi Mangione is expected to plead guilty on Friday to federal stalking charges in connection with the 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in Manhattan. Mangione, 28, will appear in court for a surprise hearing. Sources familiar with the matter indicate he could plead guilty to one or both of the two stalking-related federal charges. Plea negotiations between Mangione's legal team and federal prosecutors are ongoing, and specific details of the plea are not immediately clear. Mangione could reverse his decision at any time, even during the hearing. This expected plea change comes less than a month before Mangione is scheduled to go to trial in a separate state murder case related to Thompson's death. Mangione has previously pleaded not guilty to all charges in both federal and state cases. Federal prosecutors brought stalking charges against Mangione for allegedly traveling and using surveillance to kill Thompson. The federal charges carry a maximum penalty of life in prison without parole. In January, U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett blocked the Justice Department's initial request for the death penalty in Mangione's federal case. If Mangione accepts a plea deal in his federal case, his attorneys are expected to argue for the dismissal of some or all charges in his state case. Legal experts, including NBC News legal analyst Danny Cevallos, state that New York law may bar a subsequent state prosecution for the same conduct under double jeopardy protections. New York's state constitution has its own prohibition on double jeopardy, which could affect Mangione's upcoming state trial if a federal prosecution is completed. Mitchell Epner, a white-collar attorney and former federal prosecutor, said that if a federal prosecution is completed on a matter, the state cannot prosecute the matter on those same facts. In his state case, Mangione faces eight felony charges, including second-degree murder and several counts of criminal possession of a weapon. Jury selection for the state trial is set to begin next month. A state judge in May ruled that prosecutors could use a gun and notebook recovered from Mangione's backpack during trial.
